sections.name: introduction
sections.content:
1 Introduction
Science operates as a complex, self-organizing network where knowledge propagates through publications [ 35]. Scien-
tific innovation adds negative entropy to complex scientific networks by reorganizing existing knowledge elements
or introducing new knowledge, thereby driving scientific progress [ 45,190,153]. This progress enhances our under-
standing of the natural world and human social phenomena, while also fueling technological revolutions that stimulate
economic growth and sustainable human development [ 133]. However, scientific innovation faces intertwined structural
and behavioral challenges. Despite the explosive growth of scientific literature, idea expansion remains largely linear,
creating information saturation that limits novel discoveries [ 125]. This overload, together with increasing specialization,
leads researchers to favor familiar topics and avoid risk, narrowing scientific inquiry and stifling breakthroughs [ 36].
Interdisciplinary collaboration is essential for complex problems, but disciplinary barriers and coordination costs persistarXiv:2507.11810v1 [cs.DL] 16 Jul 2025

[187,182]. Larger teams are also less likely to produce disruptive innovation [ 194]. Traditional research methods
further constrain progress due to their resource intensity and dependence on limited expertise [218].
The emergence of LLMs has given new momentum to scientific innovation. As illustrated in Figure 1, compared to
traditional AI approaches, each iterative advancement in LLMs has dramatically accelerated the pace of scientific
innovation, manifested specifically in the explosive growth of scientific publications. Algorithms such as Chain-of-
Thought (CoT) [ 192] and Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) [ 6] allow LLMs to break down
complex problems, simulate human reasoning, and align with expert feedback, allowing quick adaptation to new
scientific challenges. Multimodal learning [198, 57] lets AI systems integrate diverse scientific data, while Reasoning
Language Models (RLMs) [ 8] and multi-agent systems [ 171] further enhance scientific inference and collaborative
research. As a result, LLM-driven innovation is shifting from simple tool use to advanced reasoning and collaborative
intelligence.
Figure 1: Trends in annual publication counts for traditional AI-driven versus LLM-driven scientific innovation.
We retrieved relevant literature from OpenAlex using two distinct search strategies. For traditional AI-driven
scientific innovation, we employed the following query: (science OR scientific innovation OR scientific
discovery OR science research OR research innovation) AND (artificial intelligence OR
ai for science) NOT (large language model OR llm OR chatgpt OR gpt OR language model OR
transformer OR bert OR llama) . To capture publications related to LLM-driven scientific innovation, we used
the query: (large language model OR llm OR chatgpt OR gpt OR bert OR llama OR language model
OR transformer) AND (scientific innovation OR scientific discovery OR scientific research
OR research innovation OR ai for science OR science) .

sections.name: 1.1 the need for llms in scientific innovation
sections.content:
1.1 The Need for LLMs in Scientific Innovation
Scientific innovation comprises both scientific research and scientific discovery, each with distinct but complementary
processes. As depicted in Figure 2, scientific discovery is focused on the cyclical process of generating hypotheses,
conducting experiments, and making observations, the fundamental steps that drive the advancement of knowledge
and the formulation of new theories, laws, and concepts [ 175,144,3]. In contrast, scientific research follows a more
structured and iterative workflow: beginning with topic selection, progressing through literature review, hypothesis
generation, experimental design and implementation, result analysis, manuscript preparation, and culminating in peer
review [ 116,233,34]. This systematic approach operationalizes scientific discovery, translating conceptual advances
into validated scientific outcomes.
Trained in a vast corpus of scientific literature, LLMs possess the ability to process not only plain text but also multimodal
scientific data such as molecular structures, protein sequences, and images. This enables LLMs to synthesize cross-
domain knowledge and perform complex scientific reasoning and hypothesis generation [ 222,218,146]. Through
interactive engagement with human researchers, LLMs facilitate dialog-based scientific exploration and iterative
problem-solving. Specifically, in scientific research, LLMs can assist in experimental design, data analysis, manuscript
2

Figure 2: The dual pathways of scientific innovation-scientific research and discovery, and the evolving roles of
traditional AI and LLMs. The lower panels highlight how traditional AI and LLMs contribute across these pathways,
illustrating the shift from structured data and predefined tasks to unstructured data, natural language prompts, and
open-ended queries—ultimately accelerating scientific innovation.
writing, and peer review, thus improving research efficiency and quality [ 116,182,34]. In scientific discovery, LLMs
enable automated literature review, knowledge integration, and hypothesis generation, supporting interdisciplinary
breakthroughs [ 3,222]. From the perspective of autonomy and human-AI collaboration, LLMs are evolving from
simple information tools to active collaborators and even autonomous scientific agents, increasingly participating in and
sometimes leading various aspects of scientific innovation [175, 38, 146, 221].
Although existing surveys have made valuable contributions by examining specific aspects of LLM-driven research, they
often provide fragmented perspectives that fail to capture the holistic transformation occurring in scientific innovation.
Most critically, current taxonomies conflate scientific research, which focuses on automating existing workflows to
improve efficiency, with scientific discovery, which emphasizes the generation of breakthrough insights and the advance
of fundamental understanding. This conflation leads to imprecise categorizations and inadequate evaluation systems
that obscure the unique challenges, methodological requirements, and capability boundaries inherent to each domain.
To address these limitations, we propose a pyramidal framework that organizes the roles of LLMs in scientific innovation
at three hierarchical levels: Evaluator ,Collaborator , and Scientist as shown in Figure 3. This framework is designed on
the principle that LLMs’ capabilities in scientific innovation can be understood through three fundamental dimensions:
autonomy level, task complexity, and level of human-LLMs collaboration. The pyramidal structure captures the
progressive evolution from passive knowledge synthesis (evaluator) to active research partnership (collaborator) to
autonomous scientific discovery (scientist), with each level representing increasing independence, sophistication, and
transformative potential.
The pyramidal framework offers several critical advantages for understanding LLM-driven scientific innovation. First,
it provides a unified conceptual structure that integrates autonomy level, task complexity, and human-LLMs cooperation
patterns into a coherent taxonomy, enabling systematic comparison across different applications and domains. Second,
it establishes clear capability boundaries and progression pathways, helping researchers identify current limitations
and future development trajectories for each role. Third, it distinguishes between scientific research and discovery
processes, allowing for more precise evaluation criteria and methodological frameworks tailored to each domain’s unique
requirements. Fourth, the hierarchical organization facilitates systematic analysis of the evolving relationship between
human researchers and AI systems, from tool-based assistance to collaborative partnership to autonomous operation.
Specifically, this survey aims to: (1) provide comprehensive systematic analysis to date of LLM-driven scientific

multidimensional evaluation across all aspects of the scientific discovery process; (2) establish a theoretical foundation
for understanding the progression from human-directed AI assistance to autonomous AI-driven discovery, with clear
delineation of capabilities and limitations at each level; (3) synthesize methodological advances, evaluation frameworks,
and empirical findings across the three-role taxonomy to identify gaps, challenges, and opportunities for future research;
and (4) guide the scientific community toward responsible development and deployment of increasingly autonomous AI
systems in research contexts.

sections.name: 1.2 scope and contributions of this survey
sections.content:
1.2 Scope and Contributions of this Survey
We provide a comprehensive summary of existing related surveys in Table 1. Based on the coverage of different tasks
shown in the table, surveys can be primarily categorized into two groups: those focusing on specific stages of scientific
innovation and those covering the complete research pipeline.
Among surveys focusing on particular stages of scientific innovation, Wang et al. [182] focuses on collaboration in
the lifecycle of paper between humans and AI, Alkan et al. [3]specializes in hypothesis generation methodologies,
Ren et al. [146] concentrates on scientific agents and their architectures, and Zhang et al. [222] primarily provides
an inventory of LLM applications in diverse scientific domains. Within surveys attempting comprehensive coverage,
several adopt a process-oriented perspective, examining how LLMs apply to different research stages without abstracting
the hierarchical roles and capability boundaries of LLMs. For example, Reddy and Shojaee [144] reviews current LLM
advances in literature analysis and brainstorming, theorem proving, experimental design, and data-driven discovery.
Similarly, Luo et al. [116] explores LLM in the stages of hypothesis generation, experimentation, writing, and peer
review, while Zhou et al. [233] investigates the phases of hypothesis construction, validation, and publication. Eger
et al. [34] examines LLMs in literature search, ideation, multimodal scientific content generation, and peer review
processes. Unlike process-focused approaches, Zhang et al. [218] specifically reviews LLM-based autonomous systems
for scientific discovery.
However, scientific innovation should encompass both scientific research and scientific discovery, as research primarily
focuses on automating existing research workflows to enhance efficiency, while discovery emphasizes generating
breakthrough insights and explaining unknown phenomena, fundamentally advancing our understanding of scientific
knowledge [ 193,175,38]. Some surveys have attempted to address both scientific research and discovery domains.
Zhang et al. [221] reviews how LLMs are transforming methodologies at different stages of the scientific method,
while Zheng et al. [228] categorizes existing work based on LLM autonomy levels, distinguishing between Tool,
Analyst, and Scientist roles. Similarly, Chen et al. [19] attempts to unify both research and discovery processes under
their AI4Research framework, but their taxonomy inadequately differentiates between routine research automation
tasks and genuinely novel discovery processes, treating scientific discovery as merely another component alongside

comprehension and writing rather than recognizing its fundamentally different epistemological nature. However,
these studies conflate scientific research and scientific discovery, which is problematic because they require different
methodological frameworks, evaluation criteria, and capability assessments; conflation leads to imprecise taxonomies
and inadequate evaluation systems that fail to capture the unique challenges and requirements of each domain.
Furthermore, these surveys often provide only coarse-grained literature categorization, lacking a comprehensive
synthesis of relevant methodologies, evaluation metrics, and representative systems that would enable systematic
comparison and guide future development.
Our survey makes three fundamental contributions:
1.Comprehensive Pyramidal Framework Innovation. We introduce a systematic three-role taxonomy,
Evaluator, Collaborator, and Scientist, which covers all key aspects of scientific innovation, integrates autonomy
level, task complexity, and human-LLM collaboration in a unified structure, and extend existing mainstream
frameworks.
2.Scientific Innovation Transformation Focus. We reframe the core question from “how to use LLMs in
research” to “how LLMs can transform scientific innovation,” emphasizing paradigm disruption and novelty
creation rather than process automation.
3.Systematic Analysis Depth. We provide comprehensive analysis to date, including detailed benchmarks,
principled algorithm categorization, task complexity hierarchies, and multidimensional evaluation across key
aspects of LLM-driven scientific innovation.
4.Critical Challenge Identification and Research Orientation. We identify and synthesize the key technical,
methodological, and ethical challenges across different levels of LLM autonomy in scientific innovation. These
5

insights serve to highlight open problems, orient future research efforts, and guide the responsible development
and deployment of LLMs in science.
This survey is structured as follows. Section 2 introduces our pyramidal framework for LLM roles in scientific
innovation. Section 3 examines LLMs as evaluators, emphasizing scientific knowledge synthesis and literature quality
assessment. Section 4 analyzes LLMs as collaborators, focusing on hypothesis generation and experimental assistance.
Section 5 investigates LLMs as autonomous scientists, emphasizing independent research and discovery capabilities.
Finally, Section 6 discusses the path toward AI Scientists, addressing ethical considerations, safety, challenges, and
future directions.

sections.name: 2 different roles of llms in scientific innovation
sections.content:
2 Different Roles of LLMs in Scientific Innovation
Scientific innovation entails converting new ideas into functional applications that achieve quantifiable advancement
in technological, methodological, economic, and social spaces. Three notions encapsulate the essence of scientific
innovation. First, novelty is the proviso - new thinking or hypotheses that scientists formulate on research problems
[174]. Second, discovery generates necessary raw materials by unveiling hidden new phenomena or mechanisms [ 175].
Third, paradigm disruption follows as the final outcome, wherein several innovations collectively transform science
paradigms [194].
LLMs introduce a transformative human-AI collaboration paradigm for scientific innovation. Five steps toward Artificial
General Intelligence (AGI) are outlined by OpenAI [ 30]. These phases are chatbots (level 1), like ChatGPT, which are
best suited for natural language interactions; reasoners (level 2), which have the ability to solve compound problems
with expert-level proficiency and augment reasoning abilities; agents (level 3), which are autonomous and respond
adaptively from environmental inputs; innovators (level 4), which have the potential to come up with innovative ideas
and solutions in various fields; and organizations (level 5), where AI functions as an integrated system to facilitate
organizational goals. Morris et al. [127] offer a more refined framework by establishing five levels of autonomy for AI.
At the most basic level, AI as a tool involves human oversight, with AI automating routine subtasks. AI as a consultant
assumes a substantive but reactive role, engaged only when requested by humans. AI as a collaborator enables an
equal partnership between humans and AI, with interactive coordination of goals and tasks. AI as an expert takes the
lead in interactions, while humans provide guidance or perform supporting tasks. At the highest level, AI as an agent
operates fully autonomously. In the context of scientific research, Gao et al. [38] introduce three emerging roles of AI
in terms of levels of autonomy, hypothesis creation, experimental planning, reasoning steps, and extent of human-AI
collaboration. These are the roles of AI agents as assistants, AI agents as collaborators, and AI agents as scientists. From
a mission to enhance productivity and objectivity in scientific studies by circumventing human limitations, Messeri
and Crockett [124] present four AI visions grounded on enhancing human scientists’ capacities along the research
process: oracle, surrogate, quant, and arbiter reflecting stages of research design, data collection, data analysis, and peer
reviewing respectively. Driven by the paradigm shift in scientific discovery brought about by LLMs, Zheng et al. [228]
propose three levels of LLM autonomy in scientific discovery: tool, analyst, and scientist. At the tool level, LLMs
enhance research efficiency through task automation; at the analyst level, they demonstrate significant autonomy in data
modeling and insight generation; at the scientist level, they achieve independent exploration and discovery throughout
key research stages. Meanwhile, Zhang et al. [218] argue that LLMs introduce a scaling law to scientific discovery and
advance an AGS framework that classifies AI-driven robotic systems into six levels of capability and autonomy, ranging
from no AI involvement to fully autonomous leadership surpassing human scientists. This model spans from traditional
methods devoid of AI to the ultimate stage, where artificial superintelligent robots autonomously develop new scientific
paradigms without technological or ethical constraints.
In view of the increasing autonomy and research participation of LLMs, as well as the urgent need to clarify the
evolving relationship between human researchers and AI in scientific innovation, this study proposes a pyramidal
framework for the roles of LLMs in scientific innovation, as illustrated in Figure 4 and Table 2. By differentiating their
functions, primary tasks, and modes of human–AI interaction, LLMs are categorized as evaluators ,collaborators , and
scientists . As evaluators, LLMs synthesize, reason over, and evaluate scientific knowledge, assisting researchers in
meeting their individual information needs amidst the rapid growth of scientific publications. By providing objective and
comprehensive literature analyses, LLMs also help minimize personal biases. As active research collaborators, LLMs
support humans in idea generation, hypothesis formulation, and the design, optimization, and execution of experiments.
The synergy between the analytical breadth and pattern recognition of LLMs and the intuition and domain expertise
of human researchers drives co-creation in scientific innovation. As autonomous scientists, LLMs can independently
automate end-to-end scientific workflows and, beyond that, propel scientific innovation beyond traditional human
capabilities, opening possibilities for paradigm-shifting advances. A systematic analysis of LLMs’ evolution from
passive tools, to active collaborators, to autonomous scientists—including the associated datasets, algorithms, evaluation
6

metrics, and outcomes—enables researchers to understand what LLMs are currently capable of, what they may achieve
in the future, and the distinct challenges, opportunities, and safety risks encountered at each stage.

SKS addresses the descriptive question —What has been discovered? —while SLQA tackles the normative ques-

multimodal embeddings, this triadic loop enables LLMs to act as scalable, auditable evaluators that accelerate reliable
scientific innovation.

ScienceQA [110] evaluates multimodal reasoning across natural, social, and language science domains through
21,208 questions requiring integration of visual and textual information. The benchmark provides 90% of answers
with explanations and 84% with lectures, enabling assessment of chain-of-thought reasoning processes across mixed
modalities.
MathVista [111] assesses advanced mathematical reasoning through 6,141 examples spanning seven distinct reasoning
types including algebraic, arithmetic, and geometric reasoning. The benchmark demands sophisticated reasoning over 19
visual context types such as charts, diagrams, and function plots, targeting college-level mathematical problem-solving
capabilities.
SciBench [185] evaluates college-level scientific problem-solving through 869 multidisciplinary problems from
mathematics, chemistry, and physics textbooks. The dataset features open-ended, free-response questions demanding
multi-step reasoning and complex numerical computation, with 177 multimodal problems incorporating visual elements.
Multimodal ArXiv [84] evaluates scientific figure comprehension through 100,000 multiple-choice questions requiring
college-level reasoning about scientific visualizations from ArXiv papers. The benchmark challenges models to interpret
data trends, analyze mathematical relationships, and reason over technical elements like formulas and domain-specific
terminology.
9

SciEval [165] assesses four progressive levels of scientific reasoning based on Bloom’s taxonomy: knowledge recall,
application, calculation, and research ability. The benchmark employs dynamically generated questions to prevent
memorization, requiring genuine reasoning using scientific principles across biology, chemistry, and physics.
OlympicArena [62] rigorously evaluates advanced reasoning through 11,163 bilingual problems from international
scientific competitions. The benchmark systematically evaluates eight logical reasoning skills including deductive,
inductive, and causal reasoning, while integrating multimodal elements to test spatial, symbolic, and quantitative
reasoning abilities.
MMMU [214] assesses expert-level domain reasoning across 11,500 questions spanning six disciplines, requiring
sophisticated processes like mathematical derivations, medical diagnoses, and circuit analysis. The benchmark
challenges models to reason over 30 different image types alongside text through complex reasoning chains that mirror
human expert tasks.
SPIQA [138] evaluates scientific reasoning through 270,000 questions based on computer science papers, requiring
systems to reason across visual elements, tables, and text. The benchmark features a Chain-of-Thought evaluation
setting and introduces the L3Score metric to assess semantic quality of reasoning outputs.
GPQA [145] challenges models with 448 graduate-level multiple-choice questions in biology, physics, and chemistry
that demand specialized domain reasoning beyond internet-searchable knowledge. Questions are created and validated
by PhD-level experts, targeting complex reasoning about specialized scientific concepts requiring multi-step logical
deduction.
MicroVQA [14] evaluates research-level reasoning in biological microscopy through 1,042 multiple-choice questions
curated by biology experts. The benchmark assesses three key capabilities: expert image understanding, hypothesis
generation, and experiment proposal across diverse microscopy modalities and biological scales.
CURIE [22] evaluates LLMs’ ability to understand and reason over long-context scientific materials from six diverse
domains including materials science and biodiversity. The benchmark comprises ten tasks requiring deep domain
expertise, full paper comprehension, and solution generation in mixed formats including natural language, JSON, and
code.
SciArena-Eval [227] presents a meta-evaluation benchmark constructed from human preference data to assess model-
based evaluators’ alignment with expert judgments on scientific literature tasks. The benchmark comprises 2,000
examples across four scientific disciplines, measuring automated evaluation systems’ accuracy in identifying superior
citation-attributed responses compared to human researcher preferences.
Critical Perspective and Future Dataset Design. Taken together, the above reasoning benchmarks delineate a graded
evaluation ladder that spans from elementary multimodal QA to expert-level, long-context scientific problem solving.
Large-scale resources such as ScienceQA and SPIQA ensure statistical reliability but rely heavily on multiple-choice
formats that cannot expose reasoning chains in depth, while smaller expert suites such as CURIE or GPQA deliver
authentic research difficulty at the cost of coverage and annotation expense. Cross–disciplinary sets (e.g., SciEval,
OlympicArena) probe transfer and abstraction, yet inevitably sacrifice domain granularity; conversely, narrowly scoped
collections (e.g., MathVista, MicroVQA) offer fine-grained diagnostics but risk overfitting to siloed skills. When
selecting a benchmark, we therefore recommend a three–step fit analysis: scenario alignment—match the cognitive
target (basic comprehension vs. graduate reasoning); modality necessity—choose text–only data for pure symbolic
reasoning or multimodal suites for vision–language pipelines; and granularity budget—employ large MCQ sets for
coarse screening, then refine with open-ended expert tasks for error attribution. New benchmarks should integrate
executable outputs (code, equations) alongside natural language to measure verifiable reasoning, embed the full scientific
workflow (hypothesis →experiment →claim) to evaluate process fidelity rather than answer accuracy alone, and adopt
semi-automatic annotation pipelines blended with expert auditing to scale difficulty without prohibitive cost. Such
directions will close the current gap between benchmarked capability and real-world scientific practice.
(2) Scholarly Survey Generation
The field of automated literature review generation has been advanced by several key benchmarks, each targeting
specific aspects of the review creation process. As shown in Table 4, these benchmarks vary significantly in scale, task
focus, and domain coverage, providing researchers with diverse evaluation frameworks for different methodological
approaches.
SciReviewGen [75] formulates literature review generation as a query-focused multi-document summarization task.
The dataset comprises 10,269 computer science reviews and over 698,000 cited papers, enabling the development and
evaluation of models for generating long, coherent, and original literature reviews.

HiCaD [234] focuses on hierarchical survey generation, providing 7,600 literature review catalogues paired with
389,000 reference papers. This resource emphasizes multi-level organizational structures, supporting the synthesis of
logically organized academic surveys.
CHIME [53] targets the biomedical domain, presenting 2,174 LLM-generated and 320 expert-validated hierarchical
structures across 100 topics. By integrating human validation, this benchmark supports research on robust, topic-oriented
survey organization.
arxivDIGESTables [131] offers 2,228 high-quality literature review tables covering 7,542 research papers. The dataset
enables research on automatic table generation for literature synthesis, addressing both schema and value extraction.
arXiv2Table [184] builds on arxivDIGESTables, providing 1,957 tables and 7,158 papers in the computer science
domain, alongside 10,196 distractor papers. This benchmark is well-suited for realistic literature review scenarios that
involve information retrieval challenges.
SurveyBench [202] compiles 100 high-quality surveys from ten computer science domains, introducing Survey
Assessment Metrics for standardized evaluation. It enables comprehensive benchmarking of both human- and machine-
generated surveys based on reference quality, structural coherence, and content accuracy.
Critical Perspective and Future Dataset Design. The surveyed review–generation benchmarks collectively chart
a continuum from query-focused abstractive summarization (SciReviewGen) to hierarchical catalogue construction
(HiCaD) and table-centric synthesis (arxivDIGESTables). Large corpora with noisy abstracts (e.g., BigSurvey)
are ideal for training fluency and content coverage, yet they obscure structural coherence and factual grounding;
high-precision datasets with expert-validated hierarchies (e.g., CHIME) capture domain rigor but remain limited to
biomedicine. Although SurveyBench introduces unified metrics (SAM-R/O/C), cross-benchmark comparability is still
hampered by heterogeneous annotation schemes and reference styles. Practitioners should thus first pinpoint the output
form required—narrative review, taxonomy outline, or comparative table—before choosing between breadth-centric
(BigSurvey), structure-centric (HiCaD/CHIME), or retrieval-stress (arXiv2Table) testbeds. Future datasets ought to
align ground-truth citations to every generated claim to discourage hallucinations, capture longitudinal topic drift so
that models must track concept evolution, and provide human preference judgments over multiple candidate surveys
to enable explicit reward modeling. These improvements will sharpen evaluation fidelity and advance automated,
trustworthy scholarly synthesis.
3.2.2 Algorithms
(1) Scientific Knowledge Reasoning
Scientific innovation largely depends on the ability to synthesize complex information, apply specialized knowledge,
and conduct advanced reasoning across different domains. Scientific knowledge reasoning constitutes the cornerstone
of this process [ 22]. Compared to knowledge bases, LLMs are considered more suitable for scientific knowledge
reasoning despite their inherent susceptibility to hallucinations [ 172]. Based on knowledge types, we categorize
LLM-based scientific knowledge reasoning into explicit knowledge extraction and implicit knowledge reasoning, while
also exploring the explainability of knowledge reasoning [21].
Explicit Scientific Knowledge Extraction. Scientific literature contains directly visible structured information requiring
systematic extraction. This process divides into fine-grained knowledge extraction and key-insights extraction.
11

Fine-grained knowledge extraction retrieves specific entities and relationships from scientific text. Natural language
processing represents the most extensively explored domain for fine-grained extraction. This includes the extraction
of models, evaluation metrics, datasets, and materials, with relationships encompassing co-occurrence and semantic
connections [ 66,219]. In biomedical knowledge extraction, Hope et al. [50] develops methods for COVID-19 research
exploration through automatic extraction of biomedical concepts. This approach employs S2ORC-BERT and RoBERTa
models to recognize entities and compute semantic similarities. The system connects genes, drugs, and diseases while
mapping collaboration networks across the CORD-19 dataset. Extending this work, Zhang et al. [225] introduces
an integrated framework combining semantic graphs with knowledge graphs. This approach addresses long-distance
dependencies and domain-specific knowledge challenges in biomedical extraction. The model compresses sentences
into semantic graphs using

sections.name: abstract
sections.content:
Abstract Meaning Representation while enriching context through knowledge graphs. Wei
et al. [191] advances this direction with PubTator 3.0, an AI-powered platform for semantic searches across biomedical
texts. The system leverages transformers like AIONER and LinkBERT to recognize entities and extract relationships.
This creates a precomputed knowledge graph enabling efficient queries. In materials science, Dagdelen et al. [23]
implements a generalizable framework using fine-tuned LLMs. This approach jointly extracts named entities and
relationships at both sentence and document levels. The framework constructs structured knowledge bases from domain
literature using GPT-3 and LLaMA-2 models.
Key-insights extraction identifies valuable research information within scientific articles. This includes research
problems, methods, evaluations, results, limitations, and contributions [ 216,160]. Lahav et al. [80] focuses specifically
on extracting scientific challenges and research directions. Their method uses a PubMedBERT-trained classifier to extract
high-confidence challenges from the CORD-19 dataset. Users can retrieve scientific directions through context-based
search inputs. Complementing this approach, La Quatra and Cagliero [79] develops THExt, a transformer-based model
generating highlight sentences from academic papers. The model employs section-level contextualization to identify key
insights. Chao et al. [17] proposes SciContriExt, an extractive approach for scientific contributions. This model defines
8 contribution types and 15 fine-grained arguments through a keyword-attention fusion mechanism. For comprehensive
scientific workflow extraction, Zhang et al. [220] construct the MASSW dataset. This resource contains over 152,000
structured scientific workflows from 17 prestigious computer science conferences (1969-2024). Using GPT-4, MASSW
systematically organizes five components: Context, Key Idea, Method, Outcome, and Projected Impact. This structured
benchmark facilitates efficient navigation of scientific innovation and accelerates methodology replication. Song et al.
[160] extends these approaches by using multiple fine-tuned open-source LLMs. This method automatically extracts
comprehensive key information including aim, motivation, methods, metrics, findings, contributions, limitations, and
future work.
Implicit Scientific Knowledge Reasoning. Unlike explicit knowledge extraction, implicit scientific knowledge
reasoning requires sophisticated multi-hop inference processes that apply domain-specific reasoning principles to derive
unstated conclusions from given information. This paradigm demands models to understand intricate scientific concepts,
navigate multi-layered logical dependencies, and generate interpretable explanations while maintaining factual accuracy.
Current algorithms for implicit scientific knowledge reasoning can be categorized into three fundamental approaches:
Chain-of-Thought reasoning, tool-augmented reasoning, and multimodal knowledge-enhanced reasoning.
Chain-of-Thought reasoning establishes the foundational paradigm for implicit knowledge reasoning by enhancing
language models’ reasoning capabilities through step-by-step intermediate reasoning generation [ 192]. Jin et al.
[70] introduce explicit thought chain generation through language models that produce lectures and explanations as
intermediate reasoning steps for science question answering. Zhang et al. [217] advance this paradigm through a
self-reflective instruction annotation framework employing a critic-and-revise mechanism. GPT-4 iteratively generates,
analyzes errors, and refines reasoning chains through three sequential stages: initial generation, reflection-based
revision, and answer-hint integration. Complex pipelines have also been proposed. Zheng et al. [229] present a
four-stage LLM4SD pipeline encompassing knowledge synthesis from scientific literature, knowledge inference from
data, interpretable model training, and explanation generation. Zhong et al. [230] develop a dual-component D5 system
with hypothesis proposer utilizing goal-conditioned prompting and hypothesis validator employing automated validity
assessment. Furthermore, based on curated reasoning samples for training reasoning models, Prabhakar et al. [137]
implement a three-step algorithmic pipeline comprising Domain Adaptive Pretraining on curated scientific corpora,
Supervised Fine-Tuning with instruction alignment, and reasoning-based knowledge distillation to enhance logical
synthesis capabilities.
Tool-augmented reasoning creates modular frameworks for implicit scientific knowledge reasoning, positioning LLMs
as proficient tool-users capable of extending domain applicability rather than omniscient problem solvers. Wang
et al. [177] introduce the LCE (Language, Code, Execution) framework that seamlessly interleaves natural language
reasoning with code generation and real-time execution feedback through special token demarcation. Ma et al. [121]
propose a four-module algorithmic architecture comprising Planning, Retrieval, Action, and Execution components,
where domain-specific toolsets are dynamically retrieved and executed based on problem requirements. Skarlinski et al.
12

[157] develop an agentic Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) algorithm that decomposes retrieval and response
generation into specialized tools including Paper Search, Gather Evidence, and Generate Answer, enabling iterative
search refinement through citation graph traversal and contextual summarization.
Multimodal knowledge-enhanced reasoning integrates knowledge from diverse modalities including text, images,
and structured knowledge networks to provide rich contextual background and verifiable traceability for implicit
knowledge reasoning. Scientific papers extensively utilize tables and figures to communicate complex information [ 57].
These elements contain implicit knowledge requiring multimodal fusion for effective reasoning. Zhang et al. [224]
propose a two-stage Multimodal-CoT framework separating rationale generation from answer inference to effectively
leverage multimodal information. Wang et al. [178] develop T-SciQ with dual teaching signal generation algorithms
combining QA-CoT for simple problems and QA-PCoT for complex multi-step reasoning through strategic data mixing
optimization. Jin et al. [70] introduce HeGTa, employing Heterogeneous Graph Neural Networks to model complex
table relationships through four node types and heuristic edge creation rules, integrated with LLMs via soft prompt
injection for few-shot complex table understanding. Mondal et al. [126] propose KAM-CoT that decomposes complex
problems into multiple intermediate steps through Chain-of-Thought reasoning, separately encodes text, images, and
Knowledge Graphs and fuses them into unified feature sets for comprehensive task understanding, finally providing
accurate and reasonable answers through a two-stage approach of rationale generation and answer inference.
Critical Perspective and Future Algorithm Design. Present methods form a complementary spectrum. Explicit
extraction pipelines (e.g., PubTator 3.0, MASSW) deliver high-precision, auditable triples and are easily aggregated
into knowledge graphs, yet they depend on costly annotation, propagate NER/RE errors, and cannot surface latent
mechanisms. Chain-of-Thought reasoning brings interpretability, but is brittle: Erroneous early steps snowball, and
self-critique is still heuristic. Tool-augmented frameworks (LCE, SciAgent) tame hallucination by delegating calculus,
retrieval, or code execution to external tools, but orchestration logic is cumbersome and failure modes multiply with tool
count. Multimodal reasoning (Multimodal-CoT, KAM-CoT) uniquely captures figure- and table-bound insights, yet
training costs and modality alignment remain prohibitive. Algorithm selection should align with task demands: explicit
extraction best suits verifiable database construction; Chain-of-Thought methods are preferable for fast, explanatory
problem solving; tool-augmented agents fit numerically intensive or data-hungry settings; and multimodal hybrids are
recommended for vision-rich corpora. Future work should fuse extraction and reasoning through retrieval-augmented
Chain-of-Thought coupled with automatic verifiers, embed confidence calibration and contradiction checks to halt error
propagation, develop plug-and-play tool registries with self-discovery and fallback logic, and design unified scientific
embeddings that treat equations, spectra, and graphics as first-class citizens, enabling truly modality-agnostic reasoning.
(2) Scholarly Survey Generation
Literature reviews represent structured approaches to scientific knowledge synthesis. They consolidate and analyze
existing research across various domains. These reviews divide into three categories based on purpose, research
questions, search strategy, analysis methods, and contributions [ 158]. Systematic literature reviews apply explicit
methodical approaches to examine evidence addressing specific research questions. Semi-systematic reviews provide
topic overviews and track historical development of diversely conceptualized subjects. Integrative literature reviews
involve creative, interpretative analysis [ 129]. For mature topics, integrative reviews summarize knowledge bases,
critically evaluate findings, and expand theoretical foundations. For emerging topics, they develop preliminary
conceptualizations and theoretical models. Current LLM-supported survey generation primarily focuses on systematic
or semi-systematic reviews. The development of integrative literature reviews based on qualitative analysis remains
underdeveloped. LLM-supported literature review automation employs two distinct methodological approaches. The
first approach organizes literature into structured formats such as hierarchical structures or layered classifications. This
organization facilitates effective review generation. The second approach builds end-to-end systems with modules that
simulate human review-writing processes. These processes include literature retrieval, screening, classification, drafting,
integration, and evaluation.
Structured Literature Organization Approach. Kang and Xiong [73] categorize the use of LLMs in academic litera-
ture reviews into three steps: information discovery, information selection, and information organization. Structuring
knowledge into hierarchical mind maps highlights key insights and relationships in research topics while improving
linguistic coherence. Hu et al. [56] propose HiGTL, a framework integrating Graph Neural Networks and LLMs. It gen-
erates hierarchical taxonomies from citation graphs by clustering papers based on structural and semantic relationships.
Using pre-trained LLMs, it provides natural language representations of classification nodes, offering a clear overview
of research trends. Hsu et al. [53] introduce CHIME, which employs LLMs to organize biomedical research into
hierarchical category trees. This system extracts concise claims and frequent entities from abstracts and uses Claude-2
to create topic-specific hierarchies, presenting categories as nodes and studies as leaves, thus enhancing researchers’
ability to navigate and synthesize literature. Newman et al. [131] employs LLMs to create literature review tables. These
tables synthesize multiple input papers into a structure with patterns (columns) and values. Researchers can effectively
13

compare papers across consistent dimensions. They decompose this complex task into two key components. First,
structure generation identifies relevant shared aspects (columns) from input papers. Second, value generation extracts
appropriate values for each paper-aspect combination. Furthermore, Wang et al. [184] address real-world literature
review scenarios that contain noisy, irrelevant papers and under-specified user demands. They develop an iterative
batch-based table generation method. This approach specifically includes using LLMs to extract key information from
full-text content, processing papers in batches through random partitioning, and iterative paper selection and schema
refinement.
Beyond hierarchical approaches, Nishimura et al. [132] develop STRoGeNS, a method for generating multi-paragraph,
structured related work sections with citations and novelty statements. It groups literature by research topics and
emphasizes the target paper’s novelty, ensuring coherence and informativeness. Li et al. [90] argue that simple chain-
of-thought methods and model limitations cause LLM-generated summaries to lack comparative analysis, structure,
and key elements. To address this, they introduce ChatCite, which mimics human literature comparison workflows. It
features a key element extractor using seven guiding questions to identify critical details and a reflective incremental
generator with two components: a comparative summarizer for iterative summary generation via comparative analysis,
and a reflective evaluator that uses LLMs to vote, screen, and rank candidate papers. Zhang et al. [223] propose
Collaborative Knowledge Minigraph Agents (CKMAs) to automate scholarly literature reviews through graph-based
approach. This framework employs a Knowledge Minigraph Construction Agent (KMCA) that uses prompt-based
algorithms to identify relations between scientific concepts and automatically construct small-scale knowledge graphs
specific to the referenced papers. Combined with a Multiple Path Summarization Agent (MPSA) that organizes concepts
from different viewpoints using a mixture of experts approach, the system efficiently generates comprehensive literature
reviews.
End-to-End Survey Generation Systems. Recent research focuses on automating traditional manual review processes
while addressing challenges of hallucination, knowledge evolution, and domain-specific comprehension. Integrating
RAG, Shi et al. [154] introduces UR3WG, a unified framework for reference retrieval and related work generation. This
model employs query expansion with LLMs to capture implicit context and specialized terminology. The framework’s
Lexicon-Enhanced Retrieval combines semantic similarity with lexical-level matching, utilizing multi-granularity
contrastive learning to enhance retrieval accuracy. Similarly, Agarwal et al. [1]develops LitLLM, an open-source
toolkit for automatic literature review generation using RAG and LLMs. LitLLM’s modular pipeline includes retrieval,
re-ranking, and generation phases, focusing on mitigating hallucinations by grounding the process in retrieved academic
papers. The toolkit offers zero-shot and plan-based generation options, enabling customized outputs based on user
requirements. Further, Susnjak et al. [166] automates the process through domain-specific fine-tuning of LLMs. Their
approach encompasses automatic data extraction at multiple levels and introduces unique tokens for tracking source
document responses. Their fine-tuned Mistral-7B models, particularly those utilizing NEFTune and LoRA techniques,
demonstrate superior performance in factual verification compared to pure RAG approaches.
End-to-end literature review generation systems continue to emerge. Wang et al. [186] creates AutoSurvey, address-
ing challenges of extensive research volumes and rapid publication rates. To overcome context window limitations,
AutoSurvey employs a four-stage pipeline: initial retrieval and outline generation, parallel subsection drafting, integra-
tion, and multi-model evaluation. The system generates high-quality surveys 1000 times faster than human authors
while maintaining comparable content quality. Liang et al. [91] introduces SurveyX with a two-phase pipeline. The
preparation stage utilizes keyword expansion algorithms for reference retrieval and structures citation information
into attribute trees. The generation phase executes outline generation, main body generation, and post refinement
(RAG-based Rewriting Module and Figure/Table Generation Module). Compared to AutoSurvey, SurveyX achieves
measurable improvements in content quality and citation quality. Given that LLM-generated outlines lack logical flow
and structural depth, and citations are inaccurate due to hallucinations, Yan et al. [202] propose frameworks named
SurveyForge. This framework combines heuristic outline generation with memory-driven content generation. By
analyzing human-written survey structures and integrating domain-specific articles to create balanced, hierarchical
outlines, it then employs a scholar navigation agent that decomposes complex queries into sub-queries using domain
literature. This agent prioritizes influential papers using citation counts and recency, ensuring cited literature is both
relevant and impactful, outperforming AutoSurvey in reference coverage, outline quality, and average content quality.
Critical Perspective and Future Algorithm Design. Two design philosophies dominate. Structured-organization
approaches (HiGTL, CHIME, arXivDIGESTables) excel at taxonomy clarity and cross-paper comparability, but often
omit nuanced critique, require upstream extraction accuracy, and struggle with topics lacking clear hierarchies. In
contrast, end-to-end systems (AutoSurvey, SurveyX, SurveyForge) offer hour-scale draft generation and flexible
coverage, yet still hallucinate citations, drift logically across sections, and underperform on deep synthesis or critical
appraisal. Choice hinges on purpose: structured pipelines are ideal for pedagogical maps or decision trees; end-to-end
retrieval-augmented systems suffice for rapid domain scans or first-pass reviews; a hybrid that layers structured outlining
atop iterative, retrieval-grounded drafting is necessary when both breadth and depth are required. Next-generation survey
14

engines should pair citation-aware planners with real-time fact-checkers to reduce hallucinations, track concept evolution
so that reviews remain current as literature grows, introduce multi-agent critique loops that combine summarization
with adversarial questioning to deepen analysis, and learn quality-weighted reward functions—such as the SAM-R/O/C
suite—to guide models toward authoritative, well-structured, and insightful surveys.
3.2.3 Evaluations and Results
(1) Scientific Knowledge Reasoning
In this chapter, we analyzes key benchmarks from the perspectives of task formats, task complexity, evaluation
frameworks, and human-model performance comparisons, as shown in Table 5.
Task formats. Multiple-choice questions (MCQs) are widely used, with varying complexity. For example, GPQA
contains 448 graduate-level MCQs in biology, physics, and chemistry. MathVista includes visual MCQs covering
figure analysis, geometry, and textbook questions. SciEval uses both MCQs and fill-in-the-blank formats to assess
scientific knowledge. Open-ended responses require higher reasoning ability. SciBench adopts free-response questions
for college-level mathematics, chemistry, and physics, while CURIE evaluates models’ abilities to generate structured
data, equations, code, and natural language explanations. Multimodal integration is prominent in many benchmarks.
ScienceQA combines text (48%) and image contexts (49%), with 31% of questions using both. MMMU incorporates
30 image types, such as charts, diagrams, MRI scans, and chemical structures, interleaved with text. SPIQA assesses
understanding of figures and tables from computer science papers through three distinct QA tasks. Some benchmarks
use specialized formats to target specific reasoning skills. OlympicArena covers 13 answer types, including numerical
values, code, and equations. Multimodal ArXiv challenges models to interpret scientific figures from academic papers.
Task complexity. The educational level ranges from elementary to graduate studies. ScienceQA covers elementary
to high school curricula (Grades 1–12). SciBench introduces college-level complexity with advanced computation
requirements. GPQA reaches graduate-level difficulty with “Google-proof” questions that are challenging even
for humans with internet access. The complexity of reasoning also varies. MathVista requires seven reasoning
types: algebraic, arithmetic, geometry, logical, numeric commonsense, scientific, and statistical. MMMU demands
domain-specific knowledge and advanced reasoning for expert-level challenges. Some benchmarks test long-context
understanding. CURIE features inputs averaging 15,000 words from full research papers, and SPIQA evaluates
comprehension of entire academic papers with figures and tables. International standards ensure rigorous evaluation.
OlympicArena sources problems from 62 international competitions such as IMO, IPhO, and IChO, targeting advanced
cognitive reasoning essential for hypothesis generation and interdisciplinary research.
Evaluation frameworks. Many benchmarks go beyond final answers to assess the reasoning process. ScienceQA
evaluates chain-of-thought reasoning through explanations and lectures. OlympicArena uses both answer-level eval-
uation for correctness and process-level scoring for step-by-step reasoning. Taxonomic frameworks are also used to
classify cognitive abilities. SciEval assesses four core scientific abilities based on Bloom’s taxonomy: basic knowledge,
knowledge application, scientific calculation, and research ability. OlympicArena benchmarks eight logical reasoning
skills and five visual reasoning abilities. Some benchmarks introduce specialized metrics. SPIQA proposes L3Score
(LLMLogScore) to better measure semantic similarity between answers. SciBench provides step-by-step solutions
to facilitate detailed error analysis. Cross-domain evaluation is also emphasized. MMMU covers six core disciplines
and 30 subjects, while CURIE spans six scientific disciplines including materials science, quantum computing, and
biodiversity.
Human-model performance comparisons. Persistent performance gaps are observed across benchmarks. On
MathVista, humans achieve 60.3% accuracy, while the best model (GPT-4V) reaches 49.9%, revealing a 10.4% gap.
On SciBench, models achieve only 43.22% accuracy on textbook problems and 13.8% on multimodal questions.
Task-specific challenges affect model capabilities differently. On GPQA’s graduate-level questions, non-experts achieve
34% accuracy, while GPT-4 reaches only 39%. For ArXivQA’s scientific figures, human validation yields 88.2%
accuracy on computer science questions, compared to 46.8% for top open-source models. Model architecture also has a
significant impact. Open-source models perform poorly on MathVista compared to GPT-4V . On CURIE, even leading
models like Claude-3 and Gemini Flash 2.0 achieve only 32% performance on scientific long-context tasks. Multimodal
performance remains a particular challenge. SciBench shows that model performance on multimodal subsets (13.8%) is
significantly lower than on text-only questions, highlighting the difficulty of integrating visual and textual information
for scientific reasoning.

Reference quality. Reference quality is central to scholarly survey generation, concerning both the comprehensiveness
and appropriateness of cited works. Advanced systems have developed metrics and mechanisms to ensure that survey
content is anchored to relevant primary sources. For instance, methods like QFiD explicitly optimize for the relevance
of each cited paper to chapter queries, helping generated reviews better reflect the intended scholarly landscape [ 75].
Modern models also go beyond citation presence, evaluating alignment and the semantic similarity between retrieved
and cited sources, as seen in SurveyX [ 91], AutoSurvey [ 186], and SurveyForge [ 202]. Despite notable progress,
frequent citation errors persist. Common issues include overgeneralization—where LLMs extrapolate findings beyond
cited evidence—and occasional misalignment or misinterpretation of sources [ 186]. There is consensus that improving
input granularity (e.g. leveraging full texts and citation networks, rather than abstracts alone) is vital for boosting both
coverage and precision in reference quality [75, 202].
Structural quality. Structural quality assesses whether generated surveys exhibit logical, hierarchical, and coherent
organization. Strong structure is widely recognized as essential for readability and academic utility. Approaches such as
outline optimization, attribute trees, and explicit outline heuristics are key to recent advances [ 91,202]. Models like
SurveyForge and SurveyX employ multi-stage frameworks that first plan and refine outlines before generating content,
resulting in human-comparable—and sometimes even preferred—structural quality. Hierarchical catalog generation
16

research further underscores the importance of structure, showing that second-level sections often carry the greatest
informational load and that extractive approaches struggle to capture nuanced hierarchies [ 234]. However, challenges
remain, with occasional issues like content duplication and improper nesting of subsections still evident. The adoption
of specialized metrics such as CEDS and SAM-O reflects the field’s growing appreciation for fine-grained structural
analysis [234, 202].
Content quality. Content quality encompasses various facets: topic coverage, informativeness, synthesis, critical
analysis, and factual accuracy. Human evaluations reveal that automated systems now reliably achieve solid coverage
and topical relevance, often matching or approaching expert-written reviews on these fronts [ 186,91]. However, deeper
aspects such as synthesis—connecting disparate studies—and critical analysis—offering nuanced critique—remain
less robust in generated texts, typically trailing behind human capabilities [ 91]. Informativeness and factuality are
particularly challenging when models have access only to limited paper content (e.g. abstracts), limiting their ability to
extract and synthesize detailed findings [ 75]. Catalogs and tables generated by LLMs can capture salient aspects and
novel dimensions, but there is often a trade-off between precision in reconstruction and creative insightfulness, as noted
in evaluations of scientific table synthesis [ 131]. Persistent errors include factual hallucinations, shallow summaries,
and insufficient critical perspective.
Researchers also evaluate academic survey generation algorithms from other perspectives, including traditional text
summarization metrics (ROUGE), as well as semantic relevance, fluency, non-redundancy, and knowledge utility.
Additionally, human evaluation is the most direct and reliable method for assessing the quality of generated surveys.
Measures such as Cohen’s kappa and Spearman’s correlation are used to validate inter-rater consistency and agreement
between human and automatic judgments [ 100,202]. Economic and efficiency factors are also critical: modern systems
like SurveyForge and AutoSurvey deliver large, high-quality surveys at a fraction of the time and cost required for
manual efforts, making them practical tools for accelerating domain knowledge acquisition [186, 202].
3.3 Scientific Literature Quality Assessment
3.3.1 Benchmarks
To evaluate LLMs on scientific literature quality, scholars have converged on two complementary benchmark families:
corpora that quantify innovation and breakthrough potential of published work, and datasets that capture expert peer-
review judgments across venues and disciplines. These resources supply ground-truth signals in the form of novelty
scores, rigor ratings, and multi-aspect critiques, which are essential for training or auditing LLMs on tasks ranging from
automated innovation measurement to review generation. A concise overview of the most widely used benchmarks is
given in Table 7, which can guide the selection of the data set according to the dimension of the target assessment and
the coverage of the domain.
(1) Innovation Measurement
Nobel-Winning Papers [83] compiles publication records for 545 Nobel laureates in Physics, Chemistry, and Physiol-
ogy/Medicine from 1901–2016, enabling analysis of career trajectories, discovery patterns, and features of breakthrough,
interdisciplinary, and team-based research.
H1Connect catalogs expert-reviewed medical and life science publications, including peer-reviewed ratings on rigor,
reproducibility, and innovation. The dataset provides detailed metadata and recommendation categories, serving as a
robust benchmark for identifying innovative research beyond citation-based metrics.
DeSci links OpenAlex metadata with two computed novelty scores per publication: content novelty (unique keyword
combinations) and context novelty (original reference journal mixes), offering comprehensive, objective metrics for
measuring scientific innovation.
Editorial Highlights [128] aggregates 230 annual discoveries and ∼9,000 weekly research highlights from top
journals, providing direct links to breakthrough publications. This curated set enables analysis of editorial criteria for
breakthroughs and interdisciplinary features of high-impact research.
SciSciNet [95],PKG 2.0 [197]: SciSciNet contains 134M global publications with detailed metadata, metrics, and
links to patents and clinical trials for research evaluation. PKG 2.0 covers 36M biomedical papers, 1.3M patents, 0.48M
clinical trials, and rich biomedical entity annotations. Together, they provide large-scale data for studying scientific
innovation and networks.
