Critical Perspective and Future Dataset Design. Current innovation datasets strike a useful balance between depth
and breadth: curated sets (e.g., Nobel, Editorial Highlights) deliver high-precision ground truth for “breakthrough”
status, whereas massive bibliometric graphs (SciSciNet, DeSci, PKG 2.0) enable statistically robust modeling of novelty
trajectories. The trade-off is clear: small curated corpora suffer from sampling bias and sparse temporal coverage,
while large graphs inherit citation-based confounders, domain skew, and delayed signal. When selecting a benchmark,
practitioners should match required granularity—career- or paper-level, disciplinary span—mono- vs. multi-field, and
evaluation horizon—retrospective vs. early-signal forecasting. Future resources should couple full-text, code, and
dataset artifacts with bibliometrics to capture mechanism-level originality; embed prospective, time-stamped expert
panels to validate “breakthrough” claims before citation accrual.
(2) Automated Peer Review
NLPeer [32] offers a large-scale benchmark for scientific peer review analysis, featuring 11,515 reviews and 5,672
papers across five venues with both blind (e.g., ACL Rolling Review, COLING) and open (e.g., F1000Research) review
formats. It provides versioned documents, rich metadata, and Intertextual Graph (ITG) structures for cross-document
modeling. Supporting tasks like review score prediction, sentence-level classification, and guided skimming, NLPeer
enables fine-grained evaluation of LLMs in review quality and scientific discourse modeling.
ASAP-Review [213] supports fine-grained assessment of review generation and quality assessment, spanning 28,119
reviews across 8,877 ICLR and NeurIPS papers. It provides aspect-level annotations (e.g., originality, clarity) and
sentiment labels, with 1,000 reviews manually labeled and the rest heuristically tagged. The benchmark formulates
review writing as aspect-aware summarization and introduces a multi-dimensional evaluation covering decisiveness,
justification, and factuality. It supports bias analysis based on author identity factors such as nativeness and anonymity.
PEERSUM [86] is the benchmark for abstractive meta-review generation framed as multi-document summarization
with conversational structure. It includes 14,993 instances from ICLR and NeurIPS, each comprising reviews, author
responses, and discussions, paired with meta-reviews from area chairs. Annotated with review scores, confidence,
18

and decisions, it supports both summarization and metadata prediction. With 13.6% of cases involving reviewer
disagreement, PEERSUM enables research on conflict-aware generation and meta-evaluation in peer review.
MOPRD [94] provides structured annotations for open peer review research, featuring 6,578 papers and 22,483 review
comments from PeerJ journals across biology, chemistry, CS, and medicine. It includes full review pipelines with
rebuttals, meta-reviews, and editorial decisions. Review comments are categorized into four aspects (basic reporting,
experimental design, validity of findings and additional comments) and auto-labeled for fine-grained analysis. The
benchmark supports structured generation and review understanding across diverse scientific disciplines.
ReviewCritique [28] benchmarks LLM capabilities in reviewing and meta-reviewing NLP papers, featuring 100
papers from ICLR and NeurIPS with 380 human reviews, 60 LLM reviews, and full peer review materials. It includes
938 annotated deficiencies across 23 fine-grained error types and supports tasks like quality assessment, meta-review
generation, and error detection.
REVIEWER2 [40] consists of 27,805 papers and 99,727 reviews from six leading NLP and ML conferences. It
provides full texts, meta-reviews, and structured metadata, and introduces 97,960 aspect-specific prompts to guide
controlled review generation.
RR-MCQ [231] facilitates research on evaluating LLMs as scientific paper reviewers via 196 multiple-choice questions
derived from 55 reviews on 14 ICLR 2023 papers. Each question is annotated with 788 fine-grained labels across review
dimensions, required abilities, and external knowledge needs. The benchmark uses a two-step evaluation where models
first locate relevant text before selecting an answer.
Critical Perspective and Future Dataset Design. Peer-review corpora provide rich supervision signals—multi-aspect
ratings (ASAP-Review), dialogue threads (PEERSUM, MOPRD), and deficiency tags (ReviewCritique)—yet they
remain concentrated in NLP/ML venues and often rely on heuristic or crowd annotations that blur expert consensus.
Scale versus fidelity is again the key tension: NLPeer and REVIEWER2 offer tens of thousands of reviews but
vary in label quality, while ReviewCritique yields gold labels at the cost of coverage. Dataset choice should depend
on desired granularity—sentence, aspect, or whole-review; context length—abstract-based vs. full-paper; and task
focus—generation, scoring, or error detection. Next-generation benchmarks should extend to under-represented
disciplines, preserve double-blind metadata for bias audits, include structured review rubrics aligned with editorial
guidelines, and incorporate longitudinal decision outcomes to link critique quality with downstream impact.
3.3.2 Algorithms
(1) Innovation Measurement
Measurement based on knowledge recombination. In the field of innovation measurement, the theory of combination
of atypical novelty serves as the primary guiding principle [ 188,226]. This theory posits that innovation emerges from
the recombination of existing knowledge elements rather than appearing entirely from nothing [ 174,36]. Based on this
theory, early innovation measurement research utilized pre-trained language models such as BERT, SPECTER, and
SentenceBERT to directly extract knowledge elements from the scientific literature and calculate the novelty of these
combinations of knowledge elements [ 52,4]. For knowledge element types, Luo et al. [115] refined the previously
vague and undefined knowledge elements into question-method combinations. Chen et al. [18] introduced contrastive
learning to predict the disruptive potential of question-method combinations by analyzing the differences between the
measurements in the literature and current strategies. They used Monte Carlo search algorithms to iteratively explore
combinations with high disruptive potential. Wang et al. [189] employed BERTopic topic models to categorize papers
into corresponding topic knowledge elements based on their topic distributions. For knowledge element sources, Wang
et al. [188] extended the extraction window from titles and abstracts to full texts. They classified extracted knowledge
entities common in computer science, including task, method, metric, material, other scientific term, and generic. They
constructed individual knowledge entity networks for each paper and built features at the network level to predict
paper quality. Unlike entity-level knowledge element combinations, Wu et al. [195] argued that different combinations
of IMRaD sections within papers can also be used to measure innovation. They found that the combination of the
Introduction, Results and Discussion sections performed best among various combinations of sections in improving the
prediction of the novelty score.
LLMs-driven innovation measurement. Given that LLMs possess vast knowledge and excellent reasoning capabilities,
some research utilizes them as innovation evaluators for papers. Xu et al. [200] compared LLM representations and
generation, discovering that representations from different layers within LLMs can indicate the potential value of
scientific ideas. Mid-to-late layer representations outperformed the final layer and showed higher correlation with
human judgments of paper innovation. However, more research focuses on prompt engineering to fully leverage LLMs’
generative capabilities. Lin et al. [92] hypothesized that newly published papers are more innovative than previous ones.
They employed RAG methods to query relevant papers and constructed prompt templates including abstracts of both
19

target papers and related papers, requiring LLMs to provide scores from 0 to 10. Huang et al. [60] designated Nobel
Prize-winning papers and those with high breakthrough indices as highly original papers, constructing similar papers as
control groups. They defined five types of originality: theoretical, methodological, problem-oriented, result-oriented,
and application-oriented. Through zero-shot prompting, they instructed LLMs to generate originality scores, types,
and descriptions across these five dimensions. Tan et al. [168] transformed the task of measuring paper innovation
into weighted novelty scoring based on question-answering. By dividing papers into different sections and proposing
section-specific questions as well as general questions, they required LLMs to provide novelty scores and confidence
levels for corresponding sections, achieving innovation quantification based on information-rich texts. Additionally, Liu
et al. [104] noticed that existing research confuses textual similarity with idea similarity. They used LLMs to synthesize
rephrased ideas with information equivalence, partial ideas with information reduction, and incremental ideas with
information addition for seed ideas. By extracting idea-level knowledge from LLMs to train lightweight retrievers, they
achieved alignment between ideas and concepts, enabling efficient and accurate LLM-based idea novelty detection.
Critical Perspective and Future Algorithm Design. Algorithms anchored in knowledge-recombination theory excel at
transparent, large-scale scoring: entity graphs or topic mixtures extracted by BERT/SPECTER variants offer explainable
novelty indices and enable longitudinal studies with minimal human cost (e.g., Luo et al. [115] ; Wang et al. [188] ).
Their main limitation is a dependence on noisy extraction pipelines by omitted entities or mis-typed relations propagate
directly into novelty scores, and a myopic view of creativity that reduces ideas to co-occurrence statistics. In contrast,
LLM-driven evaluators provide holistic, context-aware judgments by reading full texts and reasoning with prompt
instructions (Lin et al. [92]; Tan et al. [168] ); they capture conceptual subtlety but are vulnerable to hallucination,
prompt sensitivity, and inconsistent calibration across fields. Researchers should therefore match methods to use-case
constraints: graph-based metrics for high-throughput, reproducible screening; LLM assessors for expert panels or early-
signal forecasting where nuance matters. Future work should hybridize these strands like retrieval-augmented LLMs
that ground free-form critiques in extracted graphs, or self-consistent ensembles that average over layers, temperatures,
and prompt variants to stabilize scores. Equally important is building prospective benchmarks with time-stamped expert
labels to tune algorithms for originality detection before citations accrue, and injecting fairness diagnostics to curb field-
or language-level bias.
(2) Automated Peer Review
Aspect-Guided and Structured Review Generation. Automated peer review initially emerged as an NLP-driven
approach to emulate human judgment by generating structured critiques across dimensions such as originality, clarity,
and technical soundness. Early implementations typically relied on pre-trained sequence-to-sequence models like
BART and GPT within extract-then-generate pipelines, but they encountered challenges like factual inconsistency,
generic phrasing, and limited reviewer perspective diversity [ 213]. To overcome these issues, Gao et al. [40] proposed
REVIEWER2, a two-stage framework that first generates aspect-specific prompts and subsequently produces targeted
reviews, enhancing specificity and review dimension coverage. Additionally, Ma et al. [120] incorporated iterative
refinement into the review generation process through delta feedback mechanisms informed by scholarly metadata and
citation graphs. They identified gaps between generated drafts and high-quality references via multiple-choice QA
probing, refining subsequent drafts.
Furthermore, structured generation techniques leveraging LLMs have demonstrated significant effectiveness. LMCBert
[96] integrates GPT-4o-generated structured summaries of paper content with contrastive learning (MoCo), significantly
improving interpretability and precision in discriminating academic paper quality. Similarly, OpenReviewer [ 63]
leverages a domain-specific LLM fine-tuned on expert review data from machine learning conferences, equipped with
tailored prompting strategies and structured templates. This approach substantially surpasses general-purpose models
(e.g., GPT-4o, Claude-3.5) in generating critiques aligned closely with human reviewer standards, highlighting the
importance of domain adaptation and structured critique generation.
Multi-Agent Review Architectures. Recognizing the distributed and interactive characteristics of human peer review,
recent research has transitioned from single-model approaches to multi-agent systems. D’Arcy et al. [24] developed
MARG, a leader-worker-expert agent framework where specialized LLM agents collaboratively handle distinct paper
sections and review aspects. Bougie and Watanabe [12] further advanced this by introducing Generative Agent
Reviewers (GAR), incorporating reviewer personas, memory modules, and novelty analyses operating over manuscript
graphs to enhance review depth and consistency. Additionally, Jin et al. [71] demonstrated multi-agent simulations
of full review processes, including rebuttals and meta-reviews, uncovering biases like anchoring and authority effects
typically obscured in real-world settings. Extending this paradigm, PaperEval [ 61] introduces a multi-agent evaluation
framework where CriticAgent generates detailed, explainable evaluation criteria, and QuantifierAgent employs RAG for
comparative scoring. Variants like Multi-round PaperEval (MPE) and Self-correcting PaperEval (SPE) further enhance
robustness through iterative and autonomous refinement, demonstrating scalability and interpretability across multiple
scientific domains.
20

Knowledge-Enhanced and Grounded Critiques. To address factual grounding and interpretability concerns, recent
advancements integrate structured knowledge sources and feedback-driven refinement methods. Wang et al. [180]
introduced ReviewRobot, utilizing multi-layered knowledge graphs constructed from target papers, citations, and broader
corpus backgrounds to synthesize grounded reviews. Building upon this, Yuan and Liu [212] proposed KID-Review,
enhancing semantic alignment through citation and concept graphs alongside oracle pretraining, thereby reducing the
semantic gap between paper content and human reviews. Nevertheless, the dependency on comprehensive underlying
knowledge graphs constrains these models’ generalizability across diverse disciplines. In parallel, CLAIMCHECK
[134] benchmarks the ability of LLMs to generate claim-grounded scientific critiques, explicitly linking reviewer-
identified weaknesses to specific paper claims, verifying claim validity, and systematically evaluating advanced LLMs’
grounding capabilities, thus setting higher standards for evidence-based peer reviews.
Critical Perspective and Future Algorithm Design. Three algorithmic lines dominate automated reviewing: aspect-
guided generation, multi-agent architectures, and knowledge-grounded critique. Template-driven, aspect-guided systems
(e.g., REVIEWER2) guarantee coverage and controllability but often produce formulaic prose and miss cross-aspect
dependencies, limiting depth when evaluating unconventional work. Multi-agent frameworks (MARG, GAR, PaperEval)
boost diversity and emulate human panel dynamics, yet incur heavy computational cost and occasionally amplify
inter-agent inconsistency or anchoring bias. Knowledge-enhanced models (ReviewRobot, KID-Review) deliver superior
factual grounding, though they depend on domain-specific graphs whose construction seldom scales beyond well-curated
fields. Algorithm choice should thus consider review scope and resource budget: aspect-guided models suffice for
triage and crowd-sourcing; knowledge-grounded or agentic designs are preferable for high-stakes venues demanding
rigorous, explainable critiques. Looking forward, promising directions include retrieval-augmented, chain-of-thought
pipelines that intertwine evidence retrieval, rationale drafting, and claim verification; domain-adaptive fine-tuning
coupled with adversarial training to curb leniency and stylistic collapse; and closed-loop human-AI collaboration where
expert feedback continuously updates reviewer personas and reward models, yielding reviews that are both scalable and
on par with senior-program-committee quality.
3.3.3 Evaluations and Results
Concurrent with methodological advancements, evaluation strategies for automated peer review have significantly
evolved. Yu et al. [210] developed SEA, a modular framework standardizing human reviews, training generation
models on structured targets, and evaluating review-paper semantic alignment using mismatch scores. At a broader
ecosystem level, Tyser et al. [173] established platforms such as OpenReviewer and Reviewer Arena, benchmarking
LLM-generated reviews against expert-generated ones via expert preference analyses, consistency evaluations, and
adversarial error injections. Despite positive outcomes with powerful models like GPT-4, persistent challenges remain
in accurately identifying methodological shortcomings, ethical oversights, and borderline submissions. Studies also
highlight tendencies for leniency bias and reduced rejection rates by LLMs compared to human reviewers [ 155]. Full-
text modeling strategies have been suggested to enhance detection capabilities [ 114], yet identifying high-innovation
or high-risk research remains challenging. Consequently, while significantly boosting reviewer productivity and
transparency, automated peer review should be viewed as complementary to, rather than a replacement for, expert
human judgment.
To systematically evaluate the capabilities and limitations of automated peer review systems, recent work has converged
on a set of core evaluation categories and standardized measurement methods. As summarized in Table 8, four main
categories, Soundness, Clarity, Novelty, and Value & Impact, define the multidimensional framework to assess the
quality and reliability of peer review supported by LLM.
Within this evolving landscape, the core evaluation rubrics each play a distinct role. Soundness measures the extent
to which review comments address scientific rigor and empirical substantiation, employing metrics such as Recom-
mendation Accuracy (RACC), expert-rated informativeness, citation intent distributions, and advanced alignment with
human references [ 213,188,61,39]. Clarity pertains to comprehensibility, organization, and presentation quality,
and is typically evaluated using a combination of expert scoring, readability indices, structural text features, pairwise
ranking, and language diversity metrics [ 134,61,85,39]. Novelty focuses on whether reviews highlight the originality
or creative contributions of the paper, with automated assessments based on rubric scoring, semantic similarity, and
knowledge entity network analysis [ 115,200,188]. Value & Impact addresses the scientific significance and practical
influence of the reviewed work, incorporating regression models, citation-based features, network analysis, and direct
review-to-rating scoring [ 208,85,188]. Collectively, these categories anchor the systematic evaluation of automated
peer review and enable fine-grained comparison of both model capabilities and review quality across diverse research
domains.

3.4 Observations
Research on LLMs as evaluators bifurcates into two technical streams: Scientific Knowledge Synthesis and Scientific
Literature Quality Assessment. SKS focuses on extracting and reasoning over scientific content, whereas SLQA aims to
judge novelty and methodological soundness at the article level. The two streams have progressed rapidly yet reveal
distinct strengths and limitations.
Scientific Knowledge Synthesis. State-of-the-art systems couple explicit entity–relation extraction with implicit
reasoning modules based on Chain-of-Thought, tool use, or multi-modal fusion. Benchmark design has moved from
short, text-only tasks to long-context and figure-centric challenges that require interpretable rationales.
Capabilities
•Blending explicit extraction with implicit reasoning yields verifiable knowledge units while permitting deeper
logical synthesis.
•Retrieval-augmented and multi-agent architectures reduce hallucination and enable handling of full-length
papers that include text, tables and figures.
•Process-oriented metrics now examine reasoning traces and citation accuracy, encouraging more auditable
model behavior.
Limitation
•Robust domain understanding still relies on costly annotation or tightly coupled knowledge graphs, which
limits portability to under-resourced fields.
•Visual–text alignment remains computationally intensive, and open-source models struggle to balance effi-
ciency with accuracy.
• Heterogeneous label schemes and answer formats prevent straightforward comparison across benchmarks.
Scientific Literature Quality Assessment. Researches divides into innovation measurement, which often grounded
in knowledge-recombination theory or prompt-based LLM scoring, and automated peer review, which ranges from
aspect-guided templates to knowledge-grounded, multi-agent critique systems.
Capabilities
•Large scientometric corpora combined with expert annotations provide a broader and less citation-biased basis
for judging novelty and rigor.
•Multi-aspect LLM scorers can process large submission pools rapidly and yield consistent preliminary
assessments.
•Knowledge-enhanced and agentic models improve factual grounding, dimension coverage and self-correction,
offering a plausible path toward scalable, explainable reviewing.
Limitation
• Existing systems tend to be overly lenient on methodological flaws and high-risk claims.
•Prompt-based originality scores may vary across domains and over time, and alignment with expert opinion is
still inconsistent.
•Review datasets remain concentrated in a few AI venues; disciplinary imbalance and confidentiality constraints
limit broader generalization.
4 LLMs as Collaborators
4.1 Task Definition
Scientific innovation is an iterative process involving interconnected stages such as hypothesis generation, experimental
planning, execution, and analysis [ 175]. As depicted in Figure 6, LLMs serve as active collaborators across this
workflow. Hypothesis generation spans both the formulation of natural language explanations for observed phenomena
and the derivation of research directions by synthesizing insights from literature and structured knowledge bases [ 98].
Building on this foundation, LLMs assist in both preliminary and optimized experimental design, helping to plan and
refine experiments that test the proposed hypotheses. During experimentation, LLMs can automate procedures, guide
23

the execution process, and facilitate data collection. In the subsequent stages, LLMs contribute to the optimization
and analysis of experimental results by embedding experimental data, drawing inferences, and iteratively informing
subsequent hypotheses and experimental cycles. Through their integration at each stage, LLMs not only act as powerful
predictors and generators of hypotheses, but also function as tools for experiment design, implementation, and the
modeling of complex systems, fundamentally enhancing the scientific discovery process.

and innovation evaluation. It leverages both qualitative (e.g., helpfulness and novelty) and quantitative (e.g., ROUGE-L,

making it suitable for hypothesis study in management and psychology.

formulation, drawing on structured extractions from top-tier multidisciplinary journals. Its framework is designed for
comprehensive evaluation of LLM-driven creative discovery.

and synthetic domains. Its evaluation emphasizes the plausibility and explanatory power of generated hypotheses,
supporting both generalization and interestingness analysis.

Critical Perspective and Future Dataset Design. The investigated benchmarks cover a spectrum from large-scale,
automated datasets (e.g., SciMON, IdeaBench) to expert-curated, domain-specific resources (e.g., TOMATO, TOMATO-
Chem, ResearchBench). Large datasets offer scalability and comparison but may miss nuanced or interdisciplinary
reasoning, while smaller, expert-annotated datasets provide depth but lack breadth and generalizability. Creativity-
focused and generalization-oriented datasets (LiveIdeaBench, BioHypoGen, HypoBench) better test LLMs’ capacity for
innovation but require complex, often subjective evaluation. Key strengths include attention to novelty and multi-domain
coverage, as well as hybrid evaluation metrics. Weaknesses include limited dynamic adaptability—few benchmarks
update with new scientific trends or allow for evolving tasks—and dependence on static annotation or subjective scoring.
When selecting benchmarks, researchers should match the dataset’s scale, domain, and evaluation style to their goals:
scalable metrics for broad comparisons, or expert-annotated sets for qualitative insights. For future development,
dynamic features such as continual dataset updates, adaptive task formulations, and integration of both automated and
human-in-the-loop evaluations will be critical.
4.2.2 Algorithms
To address LLMs’ limitations as collaborators in scientific hypothesis generation, including hallucinations, lack of
domain expertise, and insufficient reasoning depth, current research has developed multiple algorithmic approaches.
These can be categorized into four main types: Knowledge-augmented generation integrates external knowledge bases
to enable evidence-based generation and provide directional guidance. Iterative refinement generation establishes
cyclical optimization mechanisms that continuously improve hypothesis quality. Knowledge-augmented refinement
combines external knowledge with model self-correction capabilities to construct modularized systems for hypothesis
generation. Multi-agent collaboration enhances the scientific rigor and novelty of hypotheses by simulating distributed
cognitive processes found in real research environments.
(1) Knowledge-Augmented Generation
Knowledge-augmented scientific hypothesis generation supplements external knowledge during prompting or the
prompting process. This helps overcome hallucinations and overly generic problems in LLM generation. Through
guidance and inspiration, it promotes evidence-based hypothesis generation by LLMs.
Knowledge types. Structured knowledge graphs represent a common knowledge type for augmentation. For example,
Wang et al. [179] constructed comprehensive background knowledge graphs in the biomedical domain. Nodes represent
scientific entities (diseases, chemicals, genes). Edges denote validated relationships (such as therapeutic effects,
negative regulation). Similarly, Xiong et al. [196] used domain-specific knowledge graphs like PubTator3. They
retrieved k-step relation chains through breadth-first search algorithms. This provides structured factual foundations
for hypothesis generation. Temporal concept co-occurrence knowledge graphs. Xu et al. [199] constructed evolving
concept graphs spanning 20 disciplines from 29 million academic papers. Concepts connect through co-occurrence
relationships. Multi-level abstraction knowledge. Gu et al. [46] proposed a four-level generalization framework. It
maps concepts to different abstraction levels: L1 for domain-specific implementation, L2 for cross-domain application,
L3 for abstract principles, L4 for universal system design principles. They extracted innovative elements from over
87,000 papers. Cross-domain knowledge connections are achieved through cosine similarity matching. Personalized
research knowledge. Gu and Krenn [47] constructed the personalized knowledge graph SciMuse. They applied RAKE
algorithm for concept extraction on 58 million research papers. GPT-4 refinement and validation yielded 123,128
scientific concepts.
Knowledge augmented methods. Graph structure and text fusion. Wang et al. [179] employed multi-head graph
attention mechanisms combined with contextual text attention. They dynamically integrated structured graph features
and text signals through gating mechanisms. Retrieval-augmented generation. Xiong et al. [196] ’s KG-CoI framework
implements a three-module architecture: KG-guided context retrieval, KG-augmented hypothesis generation, and
KG-supported hallucination detection. This method uses BM25 sparse retrievers to retrieve relevant literature from
PubMed. LLM-E agents generate keywords bridging structured KG data with free-text literature retrieval. Knowledge
recombination enhancement. Xu et al. [199] viewed concept co-occurrence in academic papers as an important way
new ideas emerge. They trained BERT-based link prediction models and T5-based concept sentence generation models
using pre-2021 data. These predict new co-occurring concepts in 2021 and generate descriptions of new concept
combinations. Similarly, Gu et al. [46] implemented structured combinatorial processes. This includes decomposition
stages (breaking innovations into core mechanisms, transferable components, abstract principles) and integration stages
(achieving component merger through problem reframing, principle hybridization, constraint analysis). Step-by-step
verification enhancement. Liu et al. [103] proposed two knowledge integration approaches: (1) providing metadata
during idea generation to guide LLMs toward feasible directions; (2) adding automatic validation during idea selection
to assess empirical plausibility of hypotheses. Xiong et al. [196] conducted step-by-step verification based on KGs.
26

They used domain-specific named entity recognition to extract entities. They checked direct relationships between
entity pairs in KGs. LLM-V agents verified alignment between claims and KG triples.
(2) Iterative Refinement Generation
LLMs excel at generating novel hypotheses, but they often struggle with inductive reasoning. Iterative refinement frame-
works address this limitation by establishing cyclical processes of hypothesis generation, evaluation, and improvement,
refining initial ideas into sophisticated, testable hypotheses while maintaining scientific rigor and novelty [183, 141].
The MOOSE Series. Yang et al. [204] proposed the foundational MOOSE framework, featuring a multi-module
pipeline comprising Background Finder, Inspiration Title Finder, Inspiration Finder, and Hypothesis Proposer, along
with three core LLM-based feedback mechanisms: present feedback for immediate refinement, past feedback for
improving earlier modules using downstream signals, and future feedback for preparing context for subsequent
modules. This multilayered feedback architecture enables the system to continuously refine hypotheses based on reality
checking, novelty assessment, and clarity evaluation. MOOSE-Chem [ 205] extended the foundational framework to the
chemistry domain, proposing that most chemistry hypotheses can be composed from a research background and a set of
inspirations, thus designing three subtasks: retrieving inspirations, composing hypotheses with inspirations, and ranking
hypotheses. Unlike basic MOOSE, they employed evolutionary algorithms that combine mutation, feedback, refinement,
and recombination processes to generate hypotheses with a high similarity to the ground truth. MOOSE-Chem2 [ 206]
formalized hypothesis generation as a combinatorial optimization problem, based on the principle that optimal solutions
can be derived from optimal solutions of subproblems, and designed a hierarchical heuristic search (HHS) method that
refines hypotheses from coarse to fine level. The algorithm decomposes the hypothesis search space into manageable
abstraction levels (including mechanism of reaction, general concepts/components needed, specific components, full
details of components, and experimental conditions), not only smoothing the reward landscape but also enabling more
effective optimization through reduced complexity and improved stability. The latest MOOSE-Chem3 [ 102] incorporates
the combination of internal LLM reasoning with experimental feedback into iterative hypothesis refinement, moving
beyond pre-experiment ranking to dynamic prioritization based on empirical results. They mathematically formalized
simulated experiments and developed a clustering-based pseudo-experimental-guided ranking method (CSX-Rank) that
optimizes hypothesis ranking through structural similarity between simulated feedback and hypotheses.
Reward-guided optimization. This class of algorithms treats hypothesis generation as a mathematical optimization
problem. They guide iterative model improvement through quantitative rewards. To enhance the quality of generated
hypotheses, Zhou et al. [232] drew inspiration from the Upper Confidence Bound (UCB) algorithm in multi-armed
bandits. They designed reward functions to balance hypothesis exploration and exploitation. During the update
phase, the top-k hypotheses are evaluated. Rewards are updated based on prediction correctness. When the number
of incorrect hypotheses reaches a certain threshold, they are added to the wrong example bank for subsequent new
hypothesis generation. Li et al. [88] proposed a hypothesis optimization framework combining Supervised Fine-Tuning
(SFT) and Reinforcement Learning (RL). In the SFT stage, the model learns foundational patterns from papers and
ideas. In reinforcement learning, generated hypotheses are optimized through multi-dimensional reward models. This
optimization is guided by fine-grained feedback across novelty, feasibility, and effectiveness dimensions.
(3) Knowledge-Augmented Refinement
Knowledge-Augmented Refinement algorithms combine knowledge-driven and self-correction processes to modularize
LLM-based scientific hypothesis generation. They consist of two key components that synergistically enhance the
quality and novelty of the hypothesis: knowledge augmentation and iterative refinement. Knowledge augmentation
supplies essential information and context, while iterative refinement improves idea quality, novelty, and scientific
validity.
Knowledge augmentation component. The knowledge augmentation component serves as the foundational mechanism
for incorporating external scientific knowledge into the hypothesis generation process. Current research employs diverse
strategies for knowledge acquisition, representation, and integration in knowledge augmentation components. First
is multi-source knowledge integration. SciMON [ 181] designed multi-source integration that fused semantic graphs,
knowledge graphs, and citation graphs. The system’s semantic neighbors module used SentenceBERT embeddings to
retrieve contextually similar problems and solutions. The knowledge graph neighbors module leveraged structured
scientific knowledge graphs to identify adjacent nodes representing tasks, methods, and their relationships. The citation
neighbors module exploited citation networks to discover relevant papers through semantic similarity matching. Li
et al. [85] introduced a novel approach to temporal organization through the extension of the bidirectional chain. This
methodology constructed knowledge chains by identifying anchor papers and extending both forward (through citations)
and backward (through references) to capture evolutionary trajectories of research domains. Liu et al. [97] combined
theory-driven insights from the the literature with empirical patterns from observational data. Next is context-aware
knowledge extraction. ResearchAgent [ 5] implemented entity-centric knowledge augmentation by constructing sparse
27

matrices that captured cross-domain relationships between scientific entities. Scideator [ 142] employed three-facet
knowledge representation that systematically decomposed research papers into purposes, mechanisms, and evaluations.
This allowed the system to generate novel hypotheses through systematic facet permutation while maintaining conceptual
coherence. SCI-IDEA [ 76] utilized both token-level and sentence-level embeddings to extract key aspects from relevant
publications, including research objectives, methodologies, and evaluation metrics.
Iterative refinement component. The iterative refinement component progressively enhances the quality of the
hypothesis through self-correction, novelty optimization and preference alignment strategies. In self-correction and
reflection mechanisms, Nova [ 55] implemented comprehensive self-correction mechanisms through three distinct
processes: self-check for logical consistency, self-critique for quality assessment, and reflection for strategic planning.
ResearchAgent [ 5] employed multiple LLM-powered ReviewingAgents that provided structured feedback on generated
ideas. The system performed 3-4 iterative refinement cycles, with each reviewing agent using different evaluation
templates and criteria. In novelty optimization, SciMON [ 181] retrieved existing similar ideas from the literature using
similarity search, compared against novelty thresholds, and updated ideas with explicit differentiation instructions.
This process continued iteratively until sufficient novelty was achieved. SCI-IDEA [ 76] introduced Aha Moment
detection mechanisms that used both novelty and surprise metrics. Novelty was measured using cosine similarity
between semantic embeddings, while surprise was quantified using negative log-likelihood. This enabled identification
of potentially breakthrough concepts. Li et al. [85] implemented novelty-checker agents that evaluated candidate ideas
against retrieved papers and iteratively refined ideas when substantial similarity was detected. In preference-aligned
optimization, Dasgupta et al. [26] implemented three-phase training with preference optimization, including supervised
fine-tuning followed by Direct Preference Optimization (DPO). The system created automated preference datasets and
employed iterative DPO with dynamic generation. The models generated ideas on random topics, ranked them using
combined creativity and satisfaction scores, and created new pairs of preferences for continued refinement.
(4) Multi-Agent Collaboration
Unlike modular hypothesis generation systems, some research simulates real scientific research environments based
on distributed cognitive processes, designing multi-agent collaborative architectures to achieve scientific hypothesis
generation.
Architectures. Agent architectures for generating scientific hypotheses can be divided into role-based specialized
architectures and virtual research ecosystem architectures. For role-based specialized architectures, Qi et al. [139]
implemented a functional decomposition architecture with four specialized agents. The Analyst agent specialized in
systematic literature analysis and knowledge extraction. The Engineer agent focused on method design and experimental
protocol development, transforming conceptual hypotheses into actionable research frameworks. The Scientist agent
served as the synthesis coordinator, integrating insights to generate coherent hypotheses. The Critic agent assessed
proposed hypotheses against scientific validity standards. ACCELMAT [ 78] tailored four specialized agents for
materials science applications. The Hypothesis Generation Agent (HGA) focused on generating novel material property
hypotheses, while Critic Agents (CA) provided domain-specific evaluation based on materials science principles. The
Scientist Agent (SA) combined theoretical knowledge with experimental considerations, and the Evaluation Agent (EA)
implemented quantitative assessment protocols specific to materials research validation. For virtual research ecosystem
architectures, VirSci [ 164] constructed a research ecosystem and a multi-agent system for the generation of scientific
hypotheses using real-world academic datasets. The research ecosystem included past and current paper information
and author knowledge bases. In the multi-agent system, randomly selected agents became team leaders and initiated
collaboration with other agents, including collaborator selection, topic discussion, idea generation, novelty assessment,
and abstract generation.
Communication Mechanisms. Qi et al. [139] implemented structured sequential communication in which agents
interacted through predefined message formats. The Analyst agent provided structured literature summaries to the
Engineer and Scientist agents, who then collaborated to formulate hypotheses. The Critic agent received hypothesis
proposals and provided formatted feedback with evaluation criteria and improvement suggestions. ACCELMAT [ 78]
employed multicycle communication protocols in which agents participated in iterative feedback exchanges. The
system implemented structured rounds where HGA generated initial hypotheses, CA provided specific critiques, SA
offered theoretical improvements, and EA provided quantitative assessments. This process continued for multiple cycles
until consensus criteria were met. VirSci [ 164] implemented intra-team and inter-team discussion mechanisms through
dialogue to improve communication topology and improve simulation authenticity.
Critical Perspective and Future Algorithm Design. Collectively, the four algorithmic paradigms delineate a
continuum of methodological trade–offs. Knowledge-augmented generation affords robust factual grounding that
attenuates hallucinations, yet its performance is contingent upon the timeliness, completeness, and curation overhead
of external knowledge bases; in nascent or fast-moving domains, obsolete or sparse graphs risk confining the search
space to incremental advances. Iterative-refinement frameworks supply substantial inductive-reasoning depth and
28

frequently converge on highly structured, empirically testable hypotheses, albeit at the cost of pronounced computational
expenditure (multiple generation–evaluation cycles) and pronounced sensitivity to reward-function design, which may
inadvertently optimise for proxy metrics rather than genuine scientific value. Knowledge-augmented refinement
synthesises the virtues of grounding and self-correction but inherits the liabilities of both—namely, graph maintenance
demands and multicycle latency—while further introducing pipeline complexity that complicates debugging and causal
attribution. Multi-agent collaboration most faithfully emulates authentic research collectives, fostering epistemic
diversity and emergent creativity; nevertheless, it amplifies token consumption, accentuates coordination fragility, and
obfuscates responsibility as erroneous inferences propagate across interacting agents.
Algorithm selection should therefore be problem-specific: knowledge-augmented generation is preferable when
comprehensive, well-maintained knowledge graphs exist and breadth of exploration is desired; iterative-refinement is
advantageous for deep optimisation of narrowly scoped problems under generous computational budgets; knowledge-
augmented refinement is appropriate where both epistemic grounding and robustness are paramount and sustained
engineering support is available; and multi-agent architectures are most suitable for investigations that benefit from role
specialisation or the simulation of sociocognitive research dynamics. Prospective algorithmic innovation should seek
to hybridise complementary strengths, for example, agent collectives that invoke retrieval or refinement sub-modules
adaptively, and to incorporate adaptive evaluation loops that adjust objectives as projects transition from exploratory to
exploitative phases. Future research ought to reduce maintenance burdens via self-evolving knowledge graphs, enhance
reliability by embedding causal or mechanistic simulators into reward estimators, and improve accountability through
rigorous provenance tracking and transparent agent-level logging.
4.2.3 Evaluations and Results
We systematically review the evaluation framework for the current research on scientific hypothesis generation, as
summarized in Table 10. Seven core categories—Scientific Rigor, Value & Impact, Problem Alignment, Innovation
Appeal, Adaptability & Scope, Feasibility, and Clarity—collectively assess the potential of LLMs as collaborators in
generating scientific hypotheses. Each category encapsulates a distinct aspect: Scientific Rigor measures the soundness
and empirical testability of hypotheses, utilizing validity ratings, expert evaluations, and LLM-based plausibility scoring
[204,98,139]. Value & Impact addresses the prospective importance and practical utility of generated ideas, assessed
via expert significance ratings and citation-based analyses [ 139,164,47]. Problem Alignment evaluates how effectively
a hypothesis addresses the stated scientific problem, relying on relevance scoring, classification accuracy, and semantic
matching techniques [ 76,232,78]. Innovation Appeal captures originality and researcher interest, measured through
both subjective (novelty and excitement ratings) and objective (embedding distance, pairwise originality comparison)
metrics [ 204,164,148]. Adaptability & Scope assesses the diversity and consistency of idea generation across fields,
typically via fluency and flexibility scores, as well as cross-domain accuracy comparisons [ 148,105]. Feasibility
focuses on the technical and practical implementability of hypotheses, through domain expert evaluation and resource
requirement estimates [ 148,98,205]. Lastly, Clarity measures articulation and comprehensibility, using expert and
automated readability scores [98, 26, 5].
Empirical results across these dimensions reveal a nuanced picture of LLM capabilities. LLMs exhibit notable strengths
in Innovation Appeal and Clarity, frequently producing ideas that rate highly for novelty and are perceived as well-
written and accessible by both experts and automated judges [ 204,148,76]. In terms of Value & Impact and Problem
Alignment, studies have shown that LLMs can generate hypotheses that are relevant and occasionally rated as highly
significant by domain experts, especially when augmented with knowledge retrieval or multi-agent collaboration
[164,47,232]. However, these advances are counterbalanced by persistent limitations. The most prominent challenge
is the tension between creativity and practical constraints: as LLMs generate increasingly novel and creative hypotheses,
their outputs often become less feasible or scientifically rigorous. This trade-off is empirically substantiated by multiple
works. For instance, Liu et al. [98] found that no method excelled in both plausibility and novelty, with their analysis
revealing that LITERATURE-ONLY methods achieved the highest plausibility but lowest novelty, while ITERATIVE
REFINEMENT produced the most novel but least plausible hypotheses. This fundamental balancing act has also been
observed by Qi et al. [139] , who reported that zero-shot settings yield higher novelty but lower verifiability, and by
Ruan et al. [148] and Li et al. [88], who quantify the inverse relationship between novelty scores and feasibility. On
Adaptability & Scope, LLMs demonstrate competence in diverse domains, but performance gains tend to plateau even as
model sizes increase, suggesting bottlenecks in the models’ deep domain understanding [ 105,148]. Feasibility remains
a critical limitation, with all recent models consistently scoring below 0.5 on this metric and human experts frequently
highlighting the gap between imaginative output and practical execution [ 148,48,103]. While LLMs commonly
produce clear, well-structured ideas, the depth and comprehensive uncovering of meaningful patterns—hallmarks of
high-quality scientific hypotheses—still require substantial improvement, especially in complex or counterintuitive
domains [98, 205].
29

In summary, the current body of research demonstrates that LLMs, evaluated across a multi-dimensional framework,
have notable potential as scientific idea collaborators. Their ability to generate original and contextually aligned
hypotheses is promising, yet their outputs often face critical limitations in feasibility and scientific depth. Addressing
the intrinsic trade-offs between novelty, rigor, and practical implementability remains a central challenge for the next
generation of LLM-driven scientific innovation.

Critical Perspective and Future Dataset Design. Collectively, the nine benchmarks surveyed here delineate a contin-
uum that ranges from narrowly circumscribed, domain-specific resources—such as BioPlanner’s wet-lab protocols—to
broad, open-ended research suites exemplified by Curie and MLGym. Standardised “digital-laboratory” environments
(MLAgentBench, TaskBench) offer stringent controllability, repeatability, and fully automated scoring; neverthe-
less, their highly curated toolchains can obscure the idiosyncratic failure cases that arise in real-world laboratories.
Domain-centred corpora (BioPlanner, MLE-bench) furnish strong ecological validity and transparent performance
signals (e.g., Kaggle medal tiers), yet the resulting solutions often over-specialise to disciplinary conventions and
transfer poorly across neighbouring fields. Reproducibility-oriented benchmarks (SUPER, PaperBench) expose brittle
software dependencies and documentation lacunae, but their curation and evaluation remain labour-intensive, limiting
scalability. Finally, holistic scientific-reasoning suites (Curie, BoxingGym) constitute an ambitious step toward assess-
ing complete research cycles, though their handcrafted scope and relatively small sample sizes constrain statistical
power and generalisability. In selecting an appropriate benchmark, researchers should weigh the requisite degree
of agent autonomy, the congruence between benchmark domain and target application, available computational and
human-annotation resources, and tolerance for open-ended failure modes. The development of future datasets would
profit from multimodal, longitudinal traces of authentic experimental workflows, partially automated yet faithful grading
protocols, cross-disciplinary coverage that mitigates domain-specific overfitting, and mechanisms, such as periodic task
regeneration or the continual integration of newly published code, to ensure sustained relevance.
4.3.2 Algorithms
Experiments are the essential stage for hypothesis testing, falsification, and optimization in scientific research. With
LLMs demonstrating strong planning and reasoning abilities across diverse tasks, researchers are now leveraging LLMs
to drive scientific innovation. LLMs are being applied to experiment design, experimental optimization, analysis, and
automated experimentation.
Experiment design and planning constitute the initial phase where LLMs act as experimental assistants. The goal at
this stage is to bridge the gap between conceptual research questions and technical implementation. Well-designed
LLMs can help researchers formulate structured, scientifically rigorous experimental workflows and translate broad
ideas into actionable, technical steps, thus accelerating the path from hypothesis to experimental validation.
In biomedical and biomolecular research, LLMs can serve as experimental assistants by integrating domain-specific
knowledge with multimodal capabilities. For gene-editing experiments, CRISPR-GPT exemplifies a tailored architecture
with a four-component system: an LLM Planner for task configuration, a Tool Provider for external data access, a
Task Executor with 22 state machines for guiding experimental steps, and an LLM Agent for user interaction [ 58].
This system supports Meta, Auto, and Q&A modes, outperforming general-purpose LLMs in accuracy for CRISPR
workflows. Similarly, in biomolecular research, InstructBioMol employs a motif-guided multimodal feature extraction
module to align natural language with molecular and protein structures [ 235]. Built on Llama-2-7B, it undergoes
continual pretraining and two-stage instruction-tuning, enhancing molecule and protein design tasks. Additionally, for
antibody engineering, PALM-H3 uses a transformer-based model pre-trained on vast antibody sequences, paired with
A2binder for binding specificity prediction, enabling de novo antibody generation [49].
In chemistry and molecular discovery, LLMs can enhance experimental design by integrating with evolutionary
algorithms. MOLLEO redefines traditional crossover and mutation operations in evolutionary algorithms using
chemistry-aware LLMs like GPT-4 to generate targeted molecular structures [ 176]. Built on the Graph-GA framework,
it reduces evaluation costs and improves solution quality across tasks like property optimization and protein inhibition.
For materials science and engineering, LLMs as experimental assistants benefit from human-AI collaboration, modular
systems, and knowledge-enhanced architectures.
In mechanical metamaterial design, MetaScientist uses a two-phase approach with a domain-specific foundation model
for hypothesis generation via Socratic questioning and a 3D diffusion model for structure synthesis, incorporating human
feedback for feasibility [ 140]. In metal-organic framework (MOF) research, ChatMOF employs a three-component
system-Agent, Toolkit, and Evaluator-to handle natural language queries for property prediction and MOF generation
with high accuracy [ 74]. Additionally, in materials mechanics, MechGPT integrates retrieval-augmented generation
with ontological knowledge graphs and multiagent AI strategies, using techniques like Tree-of-Thought prompting for
refined problem-solving and simulation execution [13].
Experimental optimization and analysis is a process of iterative refinement of hypotheses, experimental conditions,
and analytical frameworks. It aims to achieve desired scientific outcomes within complex parameter spaces [ 175]. As
32

experimental assistants, LLMs enable automation and efficiency in this process. They facilitate structured exploration of
vast attribute and parameter combination spaces. They rigorously evaluate results and provide evidence for subsequent
experimental iterations.
In physical sciences, LLMs serve as experimental assistants through several innovative optimization frameworks. The
in-context learning approach leverages LLMs’ ability to predict catalyst properties using natural language descriptions
[143]. This method extracts uncertainty from LLM predictions for Bayesian optimization. It efficiently identifies
optimal catalysts with minimal experimental effort. The Monte Carlo Reasoner (MCR) framework enhances LLMs’
scientific reasoning through stochastic search over query variations [ 161]. MCR transforms general queries into refined
prompts. It evaluates outcomes using domain-specific reward functions. ChemReasoner advances catalyst discovery
by combining LLMs with quantum-chemistry-based feedback [ 162]. This system formulates catalyst discovery as an
uncertain search environment. An LLM-powered agent explores the chemical space guided by atomistic graph neural
networks. The framework features both expert-defined descriptors and LLM-generated actions. For quantum physics
applications, carefully designed prompts guide LLMs through multi-step calculations like the Hartree-Fock method
[136]. Materials science applications benefit from the Scientific Generative Agent (SGA) framework [ 119]. SGA
implements bilevel optimization where LLMs propose hypotheses while simulations provide feedback. LLMs handle
discrete components like physics equations while simulations optimize continuous parameters through gradient-based
methods.
In pharmaceutical research, LLMs enhance drug discovery through multiple approaches. ChatDrug leverages con-
versational capabilities through three modules: prompt design for domain-specific guidance, retrieval and domain
feedback for refinement, and a conversation module for iterative improvement [ 99]. This approach outperforms baseline
methods in improving properties like solubility and binding affinity. DrugAssist offers interactive molecule optimization
through a fine-tuned LLM based on Llama2-7B-Chat [ 207]. The model enables domain experts to engage in multi-turn
dialogues for molecular structure refinement. It supports multi-property optimization and range-specific property
targets. For disease progression prediction, the ComLLM framework leverages LLMs to predict disease comorbidity
within networks [109]. The system treats diseases as nodes with links representing relationships. It implements graph
prompting incorporating network structure information and retrieval-augmented generation to enhance predictions with
domain knowledge.
In cross-disciplinary domain, the General Scientific Optimizers (GSO) framework transforms LLMs into versatile
scientific problem-solvers through bi-level optimization [ 117]. The inner level uses simulators as experimental platforms
evaluating hypothetical solutions. The outer level employs LLMs as “knowledgeable scientists” analyzing feedback and
generating new hypotheses. Model editing efficiently updates specific knowledge within the LLM without extensive
retraining. TextGrad framework introduces a method for “backpropagates” natural language feedback through AI
systems [215]. This framework enables LLMs to provide detailed, context-specific suggestions for improving various
system components, including prompts, code snippets, molecular structures, and treatment protocols. Experimental
evaluations demonstrate TextGrad’s effectiveness across diverse scientific applications, from coding challenges and
scientific question answering to molecular design and medical treatment planning.
Experimental automation and execution represent a cutting-edge paradigm in scientific innovation, where complex
laboratory protocols are systematically carried out with minimal human intervention through the integration of
computational and robotic systems. LLMs bridge natural language human instructions with executable laboratory
operations, enabling autonomous experimental workflows-from initial conceptualization to data analysis and reporting-
while ensuring precision and reproducibility.
In the domain of chemistry automation, several algorithmic approaches have emerged to facilitate experimental
execution. A modular architecture for autonomous chemical experimentation incorporates a central Planner module
orchestrating interactions between Web Searcher, Docs Searcher, and Code Execution components [ 10]. This system
employs vector search techniques for efficient navigation of hardware documentation and successfully executes complex
processes such as catalyzed cross-coupling reactions with minimal human intervention. The CLAIRIFY system
translates natural language instructions into eXtensible Description Language (XDL) [ 209]. This approach implements
a critical feedback loop between generator and verifier modules, enabling iterative detection and correction of errors in
hardware definitions and syntax. The precision pouring algorithms achieved significant error reduction compared to
baseline methods. The ChemCrow system integrates GPT-4 with 18 expert-designed chemistry tools to enable molecular
property prediction, retrosynthesis planning, and safety verification [ 118]. It employs chain-of-thought reasoning to
select appropriate tools, interpret outputs, and iterate toward solutions, successfully planning and executing syntheses
of compounds including DEET and novel chromophores. The LLM-RDF framework comprises six specialized agents
for end-to-end chemical synthesis that handle literature scouting, experiment design, hardware execution, spectrum
analysis, separation optimization, and result interpretation [149]. This framework incorporates Bayesian optimization
algorithms to maximize reaction yields and has demonstrated efficacy across diverse applications including photoredox
33

C-C coupling reactions. The ORGANA system combines LLMs with advanced robotics for chemistry experimentation,
utilizing Task and Motion Planning with scheduling via an adapted PDDLStream algorithm [ 25]. This approach
achieved a 21.1% time reduction in electrochemistry experiments through parallel execution. ORGANA’s dual-level
perception system employs computer vision algorithms to detect transparent objects and monitor chemical processes
through turbidity estimation.
In materials science, the AILA system was created for automating Atomic Force Microscopy (AFM) experiments [ 123].
This system employs specialized AFM Handler Agent and Data Handler Agent modules to coordinate microscopy
operations. AILA implements genetic algorithms for autonomous optimization of PID gains in imaging, significantly
enhancing the quality of microscopic visualization. The framework also utilizes baseline correction algorithms to
enhance step-edge detection in graphene samples. Safety protocols embedded within the system mitigate experimental
risks through restricted access to critical functions, ensuring reliable operation even with minimal human supervision.
Critical Perspective and Future Algorithm Design. Collectively, the LLM-enabled experimental assistants surveyed
herein afford unparalleled flexibility, breadth, and celerity to contemporary scientific workflows, spanning initial
hypothesis formulation and protocol specification through multimodal optimisation and fully autonomous execution.
Domain-specific architectures that exemplified by CRISPR-GPT, InstructBioMol, and PALM-H3 demonstrate the
efficacy of embedding expert priors and undertaking task-oriented fine-tuning, thereby achieving state-of-the-art
performance on circumscribed problems; such specialisation, however, necessitates access to meticulously curated
datasets, bespoke model designs, and computationally intensive training regimens. By contrast, domain-agnostic
frameworks such as MOLLEO, MCR, ChemReasoner, GSO, TextGrad, and ORGANA provide pronounced modularity,
rapid prototyping capabilities, and end-to-end automation, yet they remain vulnerable to diminished interpretability,
error propagation along extended reasoning chains, and non-trivial computational complexity. Across this algorithmic
spectrum, salient strengths include human-in-the-loop feedback mechanisms, scalable exploration of high-dimensional
parameter spaces, and seamless interoperability with simulation engines or robotic platforms; principal limitations
reside in hallucination-induced unreliability, acute sensitivity to prompt engineering, and the persistent challenge of
guaranteeing reproducibility, epistemic transparency, and operational safety in fully autonomous contexts. Algorithm
selection is thus intrinsically multifactorial: investigators must weigh task complexity, data sufficiency, precision
requirements, interpretability desiderata, and resource constraints—privileging highly specialised, fine-tuned models
when veridical accuracy is paramount, and favouring generalist systems when rapid exploration or multi-objective
optimisation predominates. Future methodological advances are likely to emanate from hybrid paradigms that fuse
explicit scientific priors, ontologically grounded knowledge representations, robust human–AI governance protocols,
and harmonised benchmarking suites, thereby enhancing reliability, generalisability, and scientific utility.
4.3.3 Evaluations and Results
The evaluation of LLMs as experimental assistants involves benchmarks across multiple disciplines and diverse
experimental tasks. This section synthesizes key findings from recent comprehensive evaluations spanning computer
science, biology, chemistry, materials science, and general experimental design (see Table 12).
In computer science, programming constitutes core experimentation activities. Kaggle, containing high-quality public
datasets, public notebooks, and ML models, has become a primary data source for numerous benchmarks and algorithm
testing. For example, MLAgentBench [ 59] evaluated agents across 13 ML tasks ranging from CIFAR-10 optimization to
recent research problems, while MLE-bench [ 16] included 75 Kaggle competitions. Evaluation results reveal significant
performance gaps between commercial and open-source models, with Claude v3 Opus achieving the best performance
in MLAgentBench with 37.5% average success rate [ 59], and o1-preview with AIDE scaffolding achieving 16.9%
medal rate in MLE-bench [ 16]. Scaling experiments show promising improvements, with performance doubling when
allowing multiple attempts [ 16]. However, current model agents remain at the baseline improvement stage, capable of
analyzing and optimizing existing solutions but unable to achieve state-of-the-art performance or generate scientific
insights [ 130]. Additionally, replication experiment success rates are influenced by task recency. Well-established
datasets achieve up to 100% success rates, while recent Kaggle challenges show 0% success rates, suggesting models
may have encountered test sets during training [ 59]. To circumvent this issue, SUPER [ 9] uses "low-profile" GitHub
repositories (median 14 GitHub stars) that lack sufficient documentation and maintenance, more accurately reflecting
real research conditions. Due to data complexity, the best-performing GPT-4o achieved only 16.3% success rate on
end-to-end repository setup tasks and 46.1% success rate on focused sub-problems. PaperBench [ 163] presents even
more challenging code replication tasks, requiring reproduction of ICML papers from full text and necessary prompts
without access to original code. Human PhD students still outperformed the best AI agents (41.4% vs 26.6% for
o1-high). For rigorous experimental evaluation, Curie [ 77] designed an Experimental Rigor Engine including: The
Intra-Agent Rigor Module safeguards reliability within individual agents by enforcing extensible rigor policies; The
Inter-Agent Rigor Module maintains methodical control over agent coordination, ensuring correct task transitions
and efficient scheduling; the Experiment Knowledge Module enhances interpretability by maintaining well-structured

36% of dangerous substance synthesis requests, while the remaining 64% were refused, often only after web searches
revealed the substance’s nature, indicating reliance on external data rather than inherent safety filters.
In other scientific fields, biological protocol planning has been evaluated through BioProt [ 135], which introduced
a novel automatic evaluation framework using pseudocode representations. In next-step prediction tasks, GPT-4
achieved 70.6% function accuracy. Sequential ordering emerged as GPT-4’s primary advantage. For complete protocol
generation, 59% of automatically generated pseudocode required no manual corrections, demonstrating practical utility.
In materials science, autonomous microscopy evaluation through AFMBench [ 123] revealed that GPT-4o achieved
92% success on documentation tasks, but only 71% on analysis tasks and 70% on calculation tasks, with an overall
20% error rate. A critical safety finding was the identification of "sleepwalking" behavior in GPT-4o, where the model
performed unauthorized actions beyond instructed scope, raising serious safety concerns for autonomous laboratory
deployment. TaskBench [ 152] evaluated task automation capabilities across scenarios including Hugging Face tools,
user-centered multimedia, and daily life APIs through stages of task decomposition, tool selection, and parameter
prediction. Task automation success depends on model reasoning capabilities and instruction tuning effects. BoxingGym
[37] implemented 10 real-world scientific experimental environments as generative probabilistic models, using expected
information gain to measure experiment informativeness, capturing how much agent-conducted experiments reduce
uncertainty about generative model parameters. Agents often failed to design informative experiments, and in some
cases, experimentation actually hurt performance due to over-correction based on limited observations. Agents showed

4.4 Observations
LLMs are increasingly employed as active collaborators across the iterative stages of scientific innovation, from
initial ideation to final analysis. Current research bifurcates into two principal applications: Hypothesis Generation
and Experimental Assistance. While each domain has demonstrated considerable progress, challenges related to the
unification of these functions, along with concerns regarding reliability, safety, and the capacity for true innovation,
remain prominent.
Hypothesis Generation: LLMs now draft testable, context-aware hypotheses by marrying retrieval-augmented
literature, structured knowledge graphs and iterative self-feedback. Algorithms like knowledge-augmented prompting,
cyclical refinement and multi-agent role play curb hallucinations and deepen reasoning, while benchmarks score outputs
for novelty, plausibility and explanatory strength.
Capabilities
•Factual Grounding and Plausibility: By integrating external knowledge bases like knowledge graphs and
citation networks, LLMs can generate hypotheses that are grounded in verified data, thereby mitigating the
risk of hallucination.
•Iterative Optimization and Refinement: Algorithmic frameworks employing cyclical generation-evaluation
processes enable the continuous improvement of initial ideas, refining them toward greater clarity, scientific
rigor, and novelty.
•Distributed Cognition via Multi-Agent Systems: Architectures that simulate collaborative research environ-
ments distribute cognitive tasks such as literature review, synthesis, and critical assessment among specialized
agents, enhancing the rigor of the generated hypotheses.
Limitations
•Bias Towards Incrementalism: A reliance on shared datasets and static benchmarks can inadvertently bias
models toward generating safe, incremental advancements rather than promoting transformative or high-risk,
high-reward ideas.
•Engineering and Debugging Overhead: The complexity of hybrid systems that combine knowledge augmenta-
tion with refinement loops increases engineering overhead and complicates error attribution when debugging
the pipeline.
•Deficiencies in Causal and Mechanistic Reasoning: Despite iterative processes, LLMs often struggle with
deep causal inference and lack the domain-specific mechanistic insight required for formulating truly profound
scientific hypotheses.
Experimental Assistant: As experimental assistants, LLMs translate hypotheses into machine-readable protocols,
direct lab robots and optimize conditions via simulation feedback. Benchmarks, including BioPlanner, MLE-bench
and PaperBench, track protocol accuracy, replication fidelity and end-to-end automation, and specialized systems (e.g.,
CRISPR-GPT, ChemCrow, ORGANA) already execute full laboratory workflows with minimal human intervention.
Capabilities
•Protocol Synthesis and Execution: LLM-based agents can convert natural language instructions into structured
formats like pseudo code or extensible Description Language (XDL), enabling the coordination of complex,
multi-step laboratory operations with minimal human intervention.
•Multi-objective Optimization and Analysis: Through techniques such as in-context learning, Bayesian op-
timization loops, and simulation-driven feedback, LLMs can efficiently tune experimental parameters and
support rigorous interpretation of results.
•Enhancing Experimental Reproducibility: Benchmarks focused on reproducibility, assess the ability of LLMs
to replicate published findings, thereby stress-testing their robustness in practical research settings.
Limitations
•Operational Safety and Reliability: The opaque nature of LLM inference, together with documented “sleep-
walking” incidents in which agents autonomously execute out-of-scope actions, presents tangible hazards to
laboratory safety and experimental integrity.
