Critical Perspective and Future Dataset Design. The resources summarized in Table 13 mark a substantive advance
toward systematic assessment of LLM-mediated research, yet none affords a complete or fully authentic measurement of
scientific autonomy. AAAR-1.0 and CS-Bench provide commendable scale and fine-grained skill annotation, but their
purely textual construction precludes evaluation of tool integration, laboratory logistics, or iterative data acquisition.
LAB-Bench enhances ecological validity through protocol troubleshooting and database queries; nevertheless, its
multiple-choice format collapses rich reasoning trajectories into single-token selections, thereby diluting construct
fidelity. DSBench introduces multi-modality and executable code, but the relatively small modeling subset and reuse
of public competition data expose the benchmark to memorization and leakage risks. Scientist-Bench is distinctive
in spanning the full discovery pipeline, from hypothesis formation to manuscript generation and peer review, but its
manual curation restricts disciplinary breadth and inflates evaluation cost.
Dataset choice should therefore be dictated by the specific evaluative objective: large, heterogeneous suites (AAAR-
1.0, CS-Bench) are appropriate for breadth-oriented profiling; domain-specialized corpora (LAB-Bench, DSBench)
are preferable for depth-oriented diagnostics; and end-to-end frameworks (Scientist-Bench) are indispensable when
assessing comprehensive research autonomy. Looking forward, new benchmarks would benefit from multi-domain
coverage with explicit difficulty gradients, open-ended tasks that mandate tool invocation, iterative hypothesis testing,
and real-time data acquisition, automated, leakage-resistant scoring based on executable artifacts, and continuous updates
sourced from dynamic repositories such as pre-print servers or electronic lab notebooks. Benchmarks embodying these
principles would move the field beyond static answer accuracy and toward rigorous measurement of an LLM’s capacity
for scientific research.
5.2.2 Algorithms
(1) Fully Autonomous End-to-End Systems
Fully autonomous pipelines pursue complete procedural closure, delegating every phase of the scientific method, from
problem formulation through manuscript drafting and self-review, to one large-language model (LLM) agent or a
tightly coupled agent pair. CycleResearcher and its companion CycleReviewer demonstrate how iterative preference
optimization enables an open source policy model to draft LaTeX manuscripts while a reviewer agent provides token-
level reinforcement, thus closing the research-review loop without human oversight [ 193]. The AI Scientist extends
this paradigm by orchestrating a chain-of-thought idea generator, a code-editing assistant, a sandboxed executor
and an internal reviewer, thus generating an evolutionary “mutate–run–write–review” cycle that can generate full
research papers for less than $15 each [ 108]. Its successor, AI Scientist-v2, replaces linear iteration with a progressive
agentic tree search: an experiment manager expands promising hypotheses into branches, prunes low-utility nodes and
schedules parallel executions, thereby widening the exploratory horizon while bounding compute requirements [ 201].
Complementary systems such as Data-to-Paper emphasize traceability by decomposing the inquiry into seventeen
deterministic steps and hashing every artifact, creating a verifiable “data chain” from raw input to manuscript conclusions
[64]. In the biomedical domain, BioResearcher adopts a modular multi-agent architecture: search, literature processing,
experimental design, and programming, interconnected by retrieval-augmented generation and guarded by LLM
reviewers that veto ill-formed outputs at each module boundary [ 113]. Although these pipelines exhibit remarkable
throughput and cost efficiency, their unbroken structure heightens the risk of error propagation and fabricated results,
motivating future work on embedded verification layers.
(2) Closed-Loop Iterative Research Systems
Closed-loop frameworks embed an explicit experiment-feedback signal so that empirical observations from executed
code inform subsequent rounds of ideation. Dolphin exemplifies the approach: it ranks the literature using task
attribute scoring, generates independent ideas, implements each with exception traceback-guided debugging, and feeds
categorized performance outcomes (improve/maintain/decline) back into the prompt context, thus curbing redundant
exploration [ 211]. MLR-Copilot separates duties between an IdeaAgent and an ExperimentAgent; the latter owns an
iterative “compile–run–fix” loop whose traceback tokens are re-inserted into the code prompt until compilation succeeds
or a budget is exhausted [ 89]. NovelSeek layers specialized survey, code review, innovation and assessment agents
under a central orchestrator and maintains an idea bank encoded in embeddings to avoid semantically similar dead
ends, accelerating convergence on novel regions of the search space [170]. CodeScientist frames ideation as a genetic
39

search over (paper-snippet, code-block) tuples: crossover recombines citations, mutation appends new primitives, and
selection prefers plans that survive multi-pass execution inside an instrumented sandbox, after which a meta-analysis
agent clusters consistent wins to surface credible discoveries [ 68]. Algorithmically, these systems treat discovery as a
reinforcement or evolutionary optimization problem in which the reward signal derives from real experimental metrics;
the loop terminates when budgets, novelty thresholds, or human inspection criteria are met.
(3) Human-in-the-Loop Systems
The third class embeds algorithmic checkpoints for human or peer-agent intervention, balancing autonomy with expert
oversight. Agent Laboratory organizes role-based agents (“Ph.D.”, “Postdoc”, “ML Engineer”) that communicate
via structured messages; in co-pilot mode, researchers can inject guidance after each stage, while an LLM-based
reward model scores code snippets to steer automated refactoring [ 151]. AgentRxiv generalizes collaboration by
hosting a shared preprint server: each autonomous laboratory uploads intermediate papers, queries the repository via
sentence-embedding similarity, and augments its context with near-neighbor studies, enabling cumulative innovation
akin to the human scientific community [ 150]. AI-Researcher couples a Code Agent with a mentor-style Judge Agent;
every commit triggers static analysis and functional tests, and failures are returned with inline comments, mimicking
a continuous integration workflow entirely within LLM prompts [ 169]. Zochi [ 65] orchestrates specialized LLM
agents to autonomously generate hypotheses, run experiments, and draft research papers. Three mandatory expert-
review checkpoints gate progress, making the approach a collaborative human-in-the-loop algorithm. Carl3follows a
three-stage loop—ideate, execute, present—in which human “green-light” checks gate progression between stages,
preventing wasteful compute while preserving day-to-day autonomy. These frameworks rely on retrieval, review and
gating algorithms to share knowledge, enforce methodological standards and align the agent’s actions with ethical
norms, offering a pragmatic path toward verifiable, socially acceptable autonomous research.
Critical Perspective and Future Algorithm Design. In summary, three salient dimensions shape the practical utility
of an algorithm: degree of autonomy, epistemic reliability, and human interpretability. Fully autonomous, end-to-end
pipelines excel in exploratory breadth and cost-efficiency, yet their monolithic architecture compounds cascading error,
making them comparatively fragile with respect to hallucination, data leakage, and unverifiable inference. Closed-loop
iterative frameworks partially redress this vulnerability by coupling hypothesis generation to executable feedback,
thereby improving empirical validity and sample efficiency; however, these benefits are offset by elevated computational
overhead and sensitivity to reward-signal noise. Collaborative or human-in-the-loop systems provide the strongest
guarantees of methodological soundness, ethical compliance, and reproducibility, but their dependence on synchronous
review introduces latency and may impose cognitive and organizational burdens on expert participants.
Consequently, algorithm selection should follow a risk-adjusted decision calculus: domains with stringent regulatory or
safety constraints (e.g., biomedical discovery) warrant collaborative or hybrid closed-loop designs, whereas low-stakes,
exploratory settings can exploit the speed of fully autonomous agents. Key discriminants include acceptable error
tolerance, resource availability, clarity and stability of evaluation metrics, and institutional governance requirements.
Future algorithmic research should emphasize modular composability by separating the ideation, execution, and
verification layers. It is also important to incorporate principled uncertainty quantification, self-reflexive critique, and
cryptographically secure provenance logging throughout the system design. Integrating tree-search exploration with
learned reward models, implementing adaptive autonomy that modulates agent independence in proportion to real-time
risk assessments, and benchmarking against domain-specific open evaluation suites constitute promising pathways for
advancing robust, trustworthy autonomous science.

performance across specific research components, while providing interpretability and trustworthiness for practical

as detailed in Table 14.

more promising results, with some models achieving reasonable precision across different subtasks. Retrieval relevance

Research Planning & Ideation. Research ideation represents a critical bottleneck in autonomous scientific discovery.
Multiple evaluation studies reveal mixed results in this domain [ 89,211,107]. The AAAR-1.0 benchmark shows
that while LLMs can generate innovative experimental designs, many proposals lack feasibility or stray from original
research objectives [ 107]. Conversely, systems like DOLPHIN demonstrate successful closed-loop ideation, achieving
95% novelty rates in generated research ideas with average costs of $0.18 per idea [ 211]. Evaluation metrics such as
En-Precision and En-Recall reveal that LLM-designed experiments show innovation and diversity compared to human
designs, though practical applicability remains limited [107].
Technical Analysis & Reasoning. Technical understanding capabilities show significant variation across different
reasoning tasks. Equation inference tasks prove particularly challenging, with most LLMs performing only slightly above
random chance [ 107]. The best-performing models achieved approximately 46-48% F1 scores on equation correctness
evaluation. Visual reasoning presents even greater challenges, with models achieving near-random performance on
figure interpretation tasks [ 81]. However, table interpretation shows more promise, with Claude 3.5 Sonnet matching
human performance on TableQA tasks involving 305 questions of data interpretation from research tables [81].
Code Implementation & Execution. Code generation and execution represent areas where LLMs demonstrate
substantial practical utility. Evaluation results show remarkable success rates across multiple systems. NovelSeek
achieved 50-90% execution success rates across different task complexities, with significant performance improvements
ranging from 4 hours for biological prediction tasks to 30 hours for computer vision applications [ 170]. DOLPHIN
demonstrates 75% code execution success with automated debugging capabilities [ 211]. Cost efficiency analyses reveal
average expenses of $2.33-$13.10 per complete research implementation, representing an 84% cost reduction compared
to previous autonomous research methods Schmidgall et al. [151] .
Evaluation & Critical Analysis. The ability to conduct peer review and critical analysis remains limited for current
LLMs. AAAR-1.0 evaluations show that LLM-identified weaknesses are often superficial and lack paper-specific
depth [ 107]. However, CycleResearcher demonstrates promising advancement, achieving a 26.89% reduction in mean
41

absolute error compared to individual human reviewers in predicting paper scores [ 193]. The system achieved 74.24%
accuracy in predicting paper acceptance decisions, indicating potential for automated research evaluation.
Scientific Communication. Scientific communication, namely scientific writing capabilities, represents a strength of
LLMs. Generated papers consistently demonstrate proper scientific structure, adequate statistical analysis, and correct
data representation [ 64]. The AI Scientist framework produces complete manuscripts at costs of $10-15 per paper,
with several papers achieving scores approaching conference acceptance thresholds [ 108]. Human evaluation studies
confirm that autonomously generated papers can achieve soundness ratings of 2.69-2.71 on 4-point scales, approaching
preprint quality standards [193].
Comprehensive Research Integration. End-to-end research capabilities reveal the overall performance of current
autonomous research systems and their internal coordination and division of labor. Agent Laboratory demonstrates that
LLMs can complete entire research cycles with 80-90% accuracy for simple research goals, though complex objectives
require human co-piloting to maintain accuracy [ 151]. Multi-agent collaborative systems like AgentRxiv show that
shared research repositories enable 11.4% relative performance improvements over isolated research approaches [ 150].
Cross-domain evaluation studies, such as CS-Bench, reveal strong correlations between LLM performance in computer
science and their mathematical and coding abilities [159].

BrainBench [112] assesses the ability of language models and human experts to predict empirical outcomes in
neuroscience. Participants are presented with pairs of abstracts that share the same methods but differ in their results,
and are asked to determine which study is authentic across five subfields: behavioral and cognitive neuroscience, cellular
and molecular neuroscience, systems and circuits, neurobiology of disease, and development and plasticity.
DiscoveryWorld [67] provides a simulated laboratory containing 120 challenges in eight scientific themes (e.g.,
proteomics, chemistry, archaeology, reactor engineering, plant nutrition, space medicine, rocketry, translation), each
offered at three difficulty levels. Agents must generate hypotheses, design and execute virtual experiments, interpret
data, and act on conclusions; evaluation integrates task completion, procedural relevance, and explanatory quality.
CellBench [2] measures how well autonomous or LLM-driven agents can infer the computational analyses underlying
single-cell RNA-seq papers when given only the biological background. Derived from 50 studies and 483 manually
curated analyses, it withholds methods, asks agents to predict missing workflows, and scores predictions with micro-
and macro-averaged accuracy, isolating an agent’s capacity to propose appropriate single-cell pipelines.
Critical Perspective and Future Dataset Design. Collectively, the surveyed benchmarks constitute an important first
step toward a principled assessment of “LLMs as scientists,” offering breadth of discipline, multi-modal inputs, and
execution-based scoring. Nevertheless, several limitations temper their diagnostic power. Synthetic or heavily templated
items (e.g., portions of DiscoveryBench) may inflate apparent generalization, while small, expert-curated corpora
(BrainBench, CellBench) restrict statistical confidence and domain coverage. Most suites emphasis task completion
over deeper scientific virtues such as novelty, methodological soundness, reproducibility, and cost efficiency; evaluation
protocols rarely capture these dimensions explicitly. Dataset selection should therefore be guided by alignment with the
intended deployment context: practitioners targeting bioinformatics workflows benefit from the fine-grained pipeline
reconstruction in CellBench, whereas researchers interested in generalist planning may prefer the interactive, multi-step
challenges of DiscoveryWorld. When no single benchmark suffices, a composite evaluation drawn from complementary
datasets can provide a more balanced picture of model capability.
Future benchmark development would profit from: coupling real-world, version-controlled data with longitudinal
ground truth; incorporating multi-turn, open-ended interaction that reflects iterative scientific practice; embedding
explicit metrics for rigor, reproducibility, and resource utilization; providing tiered difficulty and domain tags to facilitate
systematic ablation; and releasing transparent scoring scripts and cost logs to support fair, reproducible comparison
across models and compute budgets.
5.3.2 Algorithms
(1) Multi-Agent LLM Laboratories
Recent studies describe LLM laboratories in which the Planner, Critic, Experimenter, and Coder function as specialized
agents working together in a cyclical workflow. This sequence starts with hypothesis generation, moves through peer
review and tool-mediated execution, and ends with reflection before the next stage of planning [ 11]. Baby-AIGS
embeds a dedicated FalsificationAgent that explicitly designs counter-experiments, thereby instilling Popperian rigor
into the loop [ 106]. Extensions such as SciAgents integrate each agent with an ontological knowledge graph; requests
for subgraphs, local reasoning, and inter-agent debate are orchestrated by a central Planner to identify information gaps
and propose follow-up queries [ 42]. Domain-focused variants adapt the generic architecture: LLMatDesign equips
agents with materials-simulation APIs plus a self-reflection module that scores every composition edit before issuing
the next modification [ 69], whereas DrugAgent maintains a two-tier hierarchy in which an Idea-space Planner drafts
alternative machine-learning pipelines and an Instructor translates them into domain-specific code by consulting curated
pharmacological libraries [ 101]. Across these systems the algorithmic scaffold is an asynchronous sequence—plan,
invoke external tools, record structured observations, critique, then re-plan—supporting hierarchical memories and
role-specific toolboxes that curb hallucinations and foster cumulative reasoning.
(2) Program-Search and Symbolic-Reasoning LLMs
A complementary line of research regards the LLM primarily as a program synthesizer that generates executable
artifacts, including functions, equations, or probabilistic programs. These outputs are subsequently evaluated by an
external system. FunSearch pairs a code-generating LLM with a deterministic scorer in an island-based evolutionary
strategy; high-scoring programs seed the next generation while inter-island cloning preserves diversity [ 147]. LLM-
SR casts equation discovery as program synthesis: the model proposes Python skeletons containing placeholders
for constants, gradient-based optimizers fit those parameters, and an experience buffer supplies top programs as in-
context exemplars to bias future sampling toward structurally novel yet performant equations [ 156]. Materials-science
adaptations add inspection and memory layers: a Formula-Generation Agent proposes expressions, a Reflection Agent
analyses past search trajectories to prune redundant operator patterns, and a depth-first search scheduler balances
exploration against exploitation while caching intermediate parses for rapid replay [ 54]. LLM4ED alternates between
43

two optimization modes—black-box self-improvement that rewrites only sub-trees of elite equations and LLM-driven
evolutionary operators such as crossover and mutation—while a complexity-penalized fitness function promotes
parsimony [ 29]. Finally, BoxLM moves beyond deterministic formulas by having a proposer LM emit PyMC programs,
an inference engine compute posterior fits, and a critic LM—primed with fit diagnostics—produce natural-language
feedback that becomes part of the next proposal, thereby realizing Box’s Loop within a language-mediated setting [ 87].
These algorithms share four pillars: a strict separation between generation and verification, persistent memories that
steer sampling based on previously evaluated artifacts, explicit diversity-preservation mechanisms such as islands or
clustering, and human-legible outputs that facilitate downstream expert refinement.
Critical Perspective and Future Algorithm Design. Multi-agent LLM laboratories exhibit marked strengths in
exploratory breadth and contextual grounding: through explicit role allocation, iterative peer-review, and ontology-
backed memories, they attenuate hallucinations and seamlessly interoperate with heterogeneous simulation or data-
retrieval tools. The concomitant liabilities are non-trivial orchestration cost, since each incremental agent or prompting
cycle compounds latency, compute expenditure, and the risk of error propagation, together with a coordination
complexity that can obfuscate accountability across the workflow. By contrast, program-search and symbolic-reasoning
pipelines enforce a rigorous separation between generative and verificatory phases, thereby guaranteeing falsifiability
and yielding concise, interpretable artifacts amenable to expert audit. Their principal drawbacks are the computational
demands of outer-loop evaluation and a propensity for premature convergence or unwieldy expressions when diversity
mechanisms are inadequately calibrated. Practically, multi-agent frameworks are preferable when the scientific
bottleneck is expansive hypothesis generation or when seamless integration with diverse domain tools is paramount;
program-synthesis approaches are advisable when formal verifiability, mathematical parsimony, or downstream human
interpretability is critical.
From a methodological standpoint, the development of new algorithms should priorities modular, declarative interfaces
among language models, external tooling, and long-term memory stores; the fusion of stochastic self-improvement
protocols (e.g., evolutionary strategies, reinforcement learning) with deterministic self-verification scaffolds; and the
encapsulation of domain priors as pluggable components. Such design principles will foster composable, reconfigurable
discovery engines capable of dynamically selecting, combining, or inventing reasoning strategies in response to the
epistemic contours of a given scientific problem.
5.3.3 Evaluations and Results
With the support of LLMs, autonomous scientific discovery has significantly expanded the capability of traditional
methods across various disciplines to search for optimal parameters within hypothesis spaces. The computational
capacity involved far exceeds human limitations. In Table 16, we enumerate current evaluation tasks and metrics across
different disciplines.
In biological sciences, LLM-based systems have demonstrated exceptional performance in complex design and discovery
tasks. The Virtual Lab framework for nanobody design achieved a 96% success rate in maintaining binding functionality.
38% of designed candidates showed high expression levels. Two nanobodies exhibited improved binding to recent
SARS-CoV-2 variants while maintaining ancestral strain compatibility [ 167]. Similarly, DrugAgent’s multi-agent
framework for AI-aided drug discovery programming achieved a 95.8% valid submission rate. It demonstrated a 4.92%
relative improvement in ROC-AUC compared to baseline ReAct methods across ADMET prediction, high-throughput
screening, and drug-target interaction tasks [ 101]. The most ambitious validation came from the AI co-scientist system.
This system not only outperformed state-of-the-art models in automated evaluations but also successfully generated
experimentally validated hypotheses. These included the discovery of KIRA6 as a novel acute myeloid leukemia
treatment candidate with nanomolar-range efficacy [44].
In materials science, LLMs have demonstrated capabilities for autonomous optimization and discovery workflows.
LLMatDesign showed superior efficiency in materials property targeting. It required only 10.8 average modifications to
achieve a 1.4 eV band gap target, compared to 27.4 modifications for random baseline methods [ 69]. The SciAgents
framework achieved novelty scores of 6-8/10 and feasibility scores of 7-8/10 across five biomimetic materials hypotheses.
Quantitative predictions included 30% crashworthiness improvements and superior electrical conductivity in graphene-
amyloid bioelectronics [ 42]. In autonomous chemical research, Coscientist successfully optimized palladium-catalyzed
cross-coupling reactions. It demonstrated systematic yield improvements and chemically sensible decision-making based
on electronic properties and structure-activity relationships [ 11]. MatExpert’s three-stage workflow achieved superior
material generation performance, demonstrating high validity rates (0.998 structural, 0.961-0.986 compositional) and
excellent property distribution alignment with significantly lower Wasserstein distances compared to baselines [ 27].
Furthermore, a multi-agent framework for materials law discovery achieved an impressive R ²correlation of 0.948 in
predicting glass formation ability using characteristic temperatures as variables [54].

In mathematics, evaluations showcase the potential of LLMs to advance fundamental research. FunSearch achieved a
landmark breakthrough by discovering the largest known cap set in 8 dimensions (512 vectors). This represents the first
improvement in this dimension and a 20-year advancement in asymptotic lower bounds for cap set capacity [ 147]. In
equation discovery, LLM4ED demonstrated remarkable accuracy with coefficient errors below 1.5% for most partial
differential equation systems. It achieved over 90% R2scores on both training and test sets for ordinary differential
equations [ 29]. The LLM-SR framework significantly outperformed traditional symbolic regression baselines. It
particularly excelled in out-of-domain generalization scenarios, maintaining superior performance even under noisy
conditions [156].
In more comprehensive cross-disciplinary evaluations, current LLM-based autonomous scientific discovery systems
reveal significant limitations despite their potential. DiscoveryBench, which covers six diverse domains, found that even
the best performing system achieved only a 25% Hypothesis Matching Score. Performance was strongly correlated with
workflow complexity and domain-specific expertise requirements [ 122]. The evaluation of ScienceAgentBench across
four scientific disciplines showed that the highest performing agent could solve only 32.4% of the tasks independently.
It reached 42.2% with OpenAI o1-preview but at ten times the computational cost [ 20]. DiscoveryWorld’s virtual
environment for complete scientific discovery cycles found that strong baseline agents struggled on most tasks. This
suggests fundamental gaps in end-to-end scientific reasoning capabilities [ 67]. In particular, even in neuroscience
prediction tasks where LLM achieved 81.4% accuracy compared to 63.4% of human experts, the evaluation focused on
pattern recognition rather than genuine hypothesis generation [112].
5.4 Observations
LLMs are increasingly formalized as scientists with two concentric mandates. Autonomous Scientific Research seeks
to optimize established procedures, including literature review, experiment planning, execution, and reporting, while
Autonomous Scientific Discovery pursues genuinely novel findings that extend the frontier of human knowledge. Despite
sharing many algorithmic primitives, such as multi-agent orchestration, tool integration, and closed-loop verification,
the two modes diverge in objectives, risk profiles, and evidentiary standards. This reveals both complementary strengths
and common methodological gaps.
Autonomous Scientific Research:
Capabilities
•End-to-end automation markedly reduces turnaround time and cost for routine analytical workflows, from data
ingestion to manuscript drafting.
•Iterative, feedback-driven loops allow agents to refine code and experimental parameters without continuous
human intervention.
•Retrieval-augmented reasoning enables more comprehensive literature coverage and context-aware decision-
making.
Limitations
•Deep domain reasoning—particularly equation verification, protocol nuance, and multimodal interpreta-
tion—remains brittle, limiting trust in unaudited outputs.
•Errors introduced early in monolithic pipelines can propagate unchecked; embedded, independent verification
layers are still nascent.
•Coordination overhead in multi-agent settings inflates computational cost and complicates provenance tracking,
especially in safety-critical domains.
Autonomous Scientific Discovery:
Capabilities
•Generative search over hypothesis space, coupled with programmatic verifiers or simulators, has yielded
demonstrable advances in mathematics, materials science, and chemistry.
•Role-specialized LLM laboratories (planner, critic, coder, experimenter) foster internal peer review and
diversify exploratory trajectories.
•Evolutionary and symbolic-regression pipelines enforce falsifiability by separating generation from external
evaluation.
46

Limitations
•Scalable validating large volumes of candidate hypotheses remains costly; partial checks risk false-positive
discoveries.
•Search procedures can converge prematurely on local optima, necessitating explicit diversity preservation and
adaptive exploration strategies.
•Cross-domain generalization is limited: systems proficient in, say, algebraic conjecture often stumble in
biological inference, underscoring the need for transferable reasoning scaffolds.
ASR systems already deliver practical efficiency gains for well-defined tasks, while ASD frameworks exhibit isolated
but compelling breakthroughs. Both strands, however, confront fundamental issues of robust reasoning, verification
rigor, and accountable deployment. Future research should priorities modular architectures that decouple ideation,
execution, and validation; incorporate uncertainty quantification; and embed cryptographically secure provenance to
enable reproducible, trustworthy autonomous science.
6 Discussion
6.1 Ethical Considerations and Safety
Ethics. The integration of LLMs into scientific innovation introduces significant ethical challenges. LLM-driven
advances may cause researchers to overestimate their true understanding of scientific phenomena, as AI-generated
explanations often appear highly persuasive. Reliance on LLMs can also foster scientific monocultures, narrowing
methodological diversity and limiting the breadth of exploratory inquiry. Furthermore, the intrinsic biases present
in LLMs risk perpetuating societal prejudices and algorithmic unfairness, which may intensify existing inequalities
[124,19,228]. As LLMs increasingly assume autonomous roles in scientific innovation, additional ethical risks emerge,
including threats to data privacy, potential content fabrication, increased risk of plagiarism, and a reduction in critical
human oversight. Collectively, these issues pose a substantial threat to scientific integrity, create opportunities for novel
forms of misuse, and complicate accountability and responsibility within the innovation process [34, 146].
Addressing these challenges requires establishing inclusive and adaptive governance frameworks that embed trans-
parency, accountability, and continuous ethical reflection into the design and deployment of LLM-driven scientific
innovations [ 82,218]. Ensuring scholarly integrity demands that researchers retain sufficient oversight and account-
ability over innovations facilitated by LLMs, thus safeguarding the reliability and validity of scientific outcomes.
Additionally, scientific innovations driven by LLMs should be guided explicitly toward benefiting the common good.
Adopting this broader sociotechnical perspective involves active public deliberation, recognition and integration of
diverse values, and continuous alignment with established ethical principles and international standards.
Safety. In addition to ethical concerns, significant safety risks arise from the growing autonomy and capabilities
of AI scientist systems. As LLMs increasingly undertake critical tasks such as hypothesis generation, experimental
design, and manuscript preparation, new risks emerge, including insufficient human oversight, potential misdirection of
scientific efforts, and the inadvertent automation of flawed research protocols [ 201,19]. Without adequate oversight,
errors or biased results produced by LLMs could remain unnoticed, emphasizing the necessity of robust governance
frameworks, transparent documentation processes, and clear attribution mechanisms throughout the scientific innovation
lifecycle.
Further, as LLM-driven innovation approaches higher levels of sophisticated agentic behaviors, potential safety threats
such as misaligned objectives, self-preservation tendencies, and deceptive actions become increasingly prominent [ 7].
These threats necessitate careful design principles that emphasize interpretability, uncertainty modeling, and explicit
constraints on autonomous decision-making. Collaborative frameworks emphasizing consistent human oversight will
be crucial to ensuring safe, responsible, and effective scientific innovation.
6.2 Challenges and Future Directions
6.2.1 Core Challenges
Model Capability and Reliability Limitations. LLMs face three tightly coupled obstacles: hallucination and factual
accuracy, domain-specific comprehension, and out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization, which together constitute the
most fundamental barrier to AI-enabled scientific innovation. First, the autoregressive training paradigm makes LLMs
prone to producing outputs that sound plausible yet are objectively false, such as citing irrelevant or nonexistent papers
during literature surveys [ 222,221]. These false results are especially dangerous in high-risk laboratory settings, where
47

they can lead to erroneous protocols and uncontrolled experimental execution [ 221]. Second, current models often fail
to grasp specialized terminology and complex concepts, for example, by misjudging critical protein-protein interactions
in biochemistry or overlooking subtle mathematical assumptions in theoretical physics [ 116]. Moreover, most scientific
LLMs are trained at a coarse field level (e.g. “chemistry”), leaving long-tailed, fine-grained topics insufficiently covered
[222]. Third, scientific test distributions routinely diverge from training data; newly coined concepts, unseen molecular
scaffolds, or proteins with novel chain counts emerge continuously, and current pretrained LLMs still struggle to handle
such shifts [222].
Lack of Transparency and Explainability. The black-box nature of current LLMs undermines scientific validation,
trust, and assimilation of AI-driven insights [ 228]. Overcoming this opacity requires a paradigm shift toward architec-
tures designed for verifiable reasoning and provable conclusions rather than superficial post hoc explanations [ 228]. In
addition, even with enlarged context windows, models often lose coherence when analyzing lengthy manuscripts, often
missing cross-sectional logical dependencies [116].
Multimodal and Multilingual Integration Difficulties. Scientific corpora span manuscripts, high-resolution images,
time series signals, code, and structured tables; each modality requires bespoke preprocessing, yet high-quality cross-
modal alignments are extremely scarce, particularly in expert-intensive domains, generating training and evaluation
costs [ 57,19]. Moreover, the English-centric bias of existing LLMs risks overlooking low-resource research areas and
hampers the integration of global data and expertise needed to tackle worldwide challenges such as COVID-19 [19].
Benchmark and Evaluation Bottlenecks. Most publicly available suites remain static, allowing models to overfit
through exposure in pre-training corpora and leaderboard gaming [ 165]. Even the newest collections seldom mirror the
full closed loop of scientific practice, from hypothesis generation to experimental verification, so systems that excel at
multiple choice or code writing subtasks routinely fail when asked to design, execute and interpret real experiments
[72]. Leakage further undermines credibility: many test questions are paraphrases of highly cited papers, making it
difficult to disentangle genuine reasoning from memorization [ 107]. Disciplinary coverage is also skewed; biology,
chemistry, and computer science dominate, whereas low-resource fields such as ecology or the social sciences receive
minimal representation, producing inflated aggregate scores that mask domain-specific weaknesses [ 122]. Multimodality
compounds the problem: vision–language tasks rarely include raw spectra, micrographs, or CAD files, so cross-modal
reasoning remains largely untested [ 81]. Finally, current leaderboards overwhelmingly reward answer accuracy,
neglecting critical dimensions such as novelty, energy cost, carbon footprint, and reproducibility, thereby encouraging
incremental gains rather than scientifically meaningful progress [ 20]. Addressing these shortcomings will require
continually refreshed, leak-resistant benchmarks that grade entire research pipelines, incorporate under-represented
modalities and disciplines, and report multi-objective metrics aligned with real scientific value.
6.2.2 Future Directions
Domain-Specific Knowledgeable Models. Future language-model development is expected to shift from broad,
“one-size-fits-all” systems toward deeply specialized models whose tokenisation schemes, pre-training corpora and
reasoning mechanisms are explicitly aligned with the primitives, ontologies and evaluation protocols of a single scientific
discipline, because empirical evidence already shows that using function-infused molecular building blocks rather than
atom-level tokens improves chemical reasoning and synthesizability [ 33], and a cross-field meta-analysis of more than
260 scientific LLMs demonstrates that performance gains are consistently largest when models are pre-trained and
benchmarked on field-specific data and tasks [222].
Integration with the Physical World. Forthcoming LLMs are expected to evolve into autonomous research
agents that couple high-level reasoning with direct laboratory control, thereby establishing a closed hypothe-
sis–experiment–data–hypothesis loop without human intervention [ 228]. Embedding planning modules in robotic
platforms gives rise to “robot scientists” capable of generating, executing, and continually refining chemical syntheses
or materials-characterization protocols [ 228]. When equipped with real-time sensing and online reinforcement learning,
such systems constitute self-driving laboratories that perform millisecond-scale feedback optimization, dramatically
reducing the search space for novel compounds and process parameters [ 19]. Moreover, embodied hybrid LLM-robot
can conduct in situ experimentation in extreme environments, deep oceans, high-radiation zones, or extraterrestrial ter-
rains, beyond the limits of human physiology [ 218]. A dual-domain workflow that screens hypotheses via high-fidelity
simulation before robotic validation further decreases experimental cost while increasing success rates [228].
Cross-Disciplinary Agent Networks. Complex scientific challenges increasingly demand knowledge that spans
multiple fields, motivating the development of multi-agent LLM networks in which domain-specialized agents cooperate
through structured message passing to execute elaborate research workflows [ 19]. Graph-based knowledge routing
enables hypotheses, variables, and results to traverse disciplinary boundaries, mitigating information silos and deepening
causal inference [ 233]. Privacy-preserving federated learning allows geographically distributed institutions to co-train
foundation models while retaining local data sovereignty, thus expanding cross-domain sample diversity without
48

compromising compliance [ 19]. Within these networks, agents dynamically assume roles in hypothesis generation,
protocol design, and data interpretation, which optimizes resource allocation and accelerates iterative discovery cycles
[228].
Human–AI Collaborative Scholarly Ecosystems. LLM agents will also reshape the social infrastructure of science
by fostering AI-native publication and review platforms. Pre-print servers such as the proposed AgentRxiv would
institute tiered review pipelines tailored to outputs generated autonomously by AI or robot scientists, guaranteeing
transparency, traceability, and ethical oversight [ 31,218]. Concurrently, intelligent peer-review assistants can flag
methodological flaws, verify citations, and deliver structured critiques, thereby decreasing reviewer workload while
maintaining scholarly rigor [ 116]. End-to-end dashboards that expose an LLM’s reasoning chain and confidence
estimates promote interoperability and enable real-time auditing of AI-derived insights [ 228]. Finally, integrating
high-quality multilingual translation and terminology alignment modules ensures equitable visibility for research in
low-resource languages, narrowing the global knowledge divide and enriching the collective scientific corpus [19].
7 Conclusion
This paper delivers a comprehensive and unified survey of the ways in which LLMs are reshaping scientific innovation.
Guided by three criteria, autonomy, task complexity, and human-AI collaboration, we position LLM capabilities within
a three-level pyramid comprising the roles of Evaluator, Collaborator, and Scientist. At the dimensions of benchmarks,
algorithms, and evaluation and results, we detail the capabilities and limitations of Evaluators in scientific knowledge
synthesis and literature quality assessment, Collaborators in hypothesis generation and experimental assistance, and
Scientists in autonomous research and discovery. The review also examines ethical considerations, identifies potential
safety risks, and outlines productive avenues for future work. We hope that this survey will serve as a practical reference
for researchers seeking to understand and responsibly advance LLM-driven scientific innovation.

1 Introduction
Science operates as a complex, self-organizing network where knowledge propagates through publications [ 35] Scien-
tific innovation adds negative entropy to complex scientific networks by reorganizing existing knowledge elements
or introducing new knowledge, thereby driving scientific progress [ 45,190,153] This progress enhances our under-
standing of the natural world and human social phenomena, while also fueling technological revolutions that stimulate
economic growth and sustainable human development [ 133] However, scientific innovation faces intertwined structural
and behavioral challenges Despite the explosive growth of scientific literature, idea expansion remains largely linear,
creating information saturation that limits novel discoveries [ 125] This overload, together with increasing specialization,
leads researchers to favor familiar topics and avoid risk, narrowing scientific inquiry and stifling breakthroughs [ 36] Interdisciplinary collaboration is essential for complex problems, but disciplinary barriers and coordination costs persistarXiv:2507.11810v1 [cs.DL] 16 Jul 2025

[187,182] Larger teams are also less likely to produce disruptive innovation [ 194] Traditional research methods
further constrain progress due to their resource intensity and dependence on limited expertise [218] The emergence of LLMs has given new momentum to scientific innovation As illustrated in Figure 1, compared to
traditional AI approaches, each iterative advancement in LLMs has dramatically accelerated the pace of scientific
innovation, manifested specifically in the explosive growth of scientific publications Algorithms such as Chain-of-
Thought (CoT) [ 192] and Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) [ 6] allow LLMs to break down
complex problems, simulate human reasoning, and align with expert feedback, allowing quick adaptation to new
scientific challenges

scientific challenges Multimodal learning [198, 57] lets AI systems integrate diverse scientific data, while Reasoning

discovery OR science research OR research innovation) AND (artificial intelligence OR
ai for science) NOT (large language model OR llm OR chatgpt OR gpt OR language model OR
transformer OR bert OR llama)  To capture publications related to LLM-driven scientific innovation, we used
the query: (large language model OR llm OR chatgpt OR gpt OR bert OR llama OR language model
OR transformer) AND (scientific innovation OR scientific discovery OR scientific research
OR research innovation OR ai for science OR science) .

1.1 The Need for LLMs in Scientific Innovation
Scientific innovation comprises both scientific research and scientific discovery, each with distinct but complementary
processes As depicted in Figure 2, scientific discovery is focused on the cyclical process of generating hypotheses,
conducting experiments, and making observations, the fundamental steps that drive the advancement of knowledge
and the formulation of new theories, laws, and concepts [ 175,144,3] In contrast, scientific research follows a more
structured and iterative workflow: beginning with topic selection, progressing through literature review, hypothesis
generation, experimental design and implementation, result analysis, manuscript preparation, and culminating in peer
review [ 116,233,34] This systematic approach operationalizes scientific discovery, translating conceptual advances
into validated scientific outcomes Trained in a vast corpus of scientific literature, LLMs possess the ability to process not only plain text but also multimodal
scientific data such as molecular structures, protein sequences, and images This enables LLMs to synthesize cross-
domain knowledge and perform complex scientific reasoning and hypothesis generation [ 222,218,146] Through
interactive engagement with human researchers, LLMs facilitate dialog-based scientific exploration and iterative
problem-solving Specifically, in scientific research, LLMs can assist in experimental design, data analysis, manuscript

Figure 2: The dual pathways of scientific innovation-scientific research and discovery, and the evolving roles of
traditional AI and LLMs The lower panels highlight how traditional AI and LLMs contribute across these pathways,
illustrating the shift from structured data and predefined tasks to unstructured data, natural language prompts, and
open-ended queries—ultimately accelerating scientific innovation writing, and peer review, thus improving research efficiency and quality [ 116,182,34]

1.2 Scope and Contributions of this Survey
We provide a comprehensive summary of existing related surveys in Table 1 Based on the coverage of different tasks
shown in the table, surveys can be primarily categorized into two groups: those focusing on specific stages of scientific
innovation and those covering the complete research pipeline Among surveys focusing on particular stages of scientific innovation, Wang et al [182] focuses on collaboration in
the lifecycle of paper between humans and AI, Alkan et al [3]specializes in hypothesis generation methodologies,
Ren et al [146] concentrates on scientific agents and their architectures, and Zhang et al [222] primarily provides
an inventory of LLM applications in diverse scientific domains Within surveys attempting comprehensive coverage,
several adopt a process-oriented perspective, examining how LLMs apply to different research stages without abstracting
the hierarchical roles and capability boundaries of LLMs For example, Reddy and Shojaee [144] reviews current LLM
advances in literature analysis and brainstorming, theorem proving, experimental design, and data-driven discovery Similarly, Luo et al [116] explores LLM in the stages of hypothesis generation, experimentation, writing, and peer
review, while Zhou et al [233] investigates the phases of hypothesis construction, validation, and publication Eger
et al [34] examines LLMs in literature search, ideation, multimodal scientific content generation, and peer review
processes Unlike process-focused approaches, Zhang et al [218] specifically reviews LLM-based autonomous systems
for scientific discovery However, scientific innovation should encompass both scientific research and scientific discovery, as research primarily
focuses on automating existing research workflows to enhance efficiency, while discovery emphasizes generating
breakthrough insights and explaining unknown phenomena, fundamentally advancing our understanding of scientific
knowledge [ 193,175,38] Some surveys have attempted to address both scientific research and discovery domains Zhang et al

2 Different Roles of LLMs in Scientific Innovation
Scientific innovation entails converting new ideas into functional applications that achieve quantifiable advancement
in technological, methodological, economic, and social spaces Three notions encapsulate the essence of scientific
innovation First, novelty is the proviso - new thinking or hypotheses that scientists formulate on research problems
[174] Second, discovery generates necessary raw materials by unveiling hidden new phenomena or mechanisms [ 175] Third, paradigm disruption follows as the final outcome, wherein several innovations collectively transform science
paradigms [194] LLMs introduce a transformative human-AI collaboration paradigm for scientific innovation Five steps toward Artificial
General Intelligence (AGI) are outlined by OpenAI [ 30] These phases are chatbots (level 1), like ChatGPT, which are
best suited for natural language interactions; reasoners (level 2), which have the ability to solve compound problems
with expert-level proficiency and augment reasoning abilities; agents (level 3), which are autonomous and respond
adaptively from environmental inputs; innovators (level 4), which have the potential to come up with innovative ideas
and solutions in various fields; and organizations (level 5), where AI functions as an integrated system to facilitate
organizational goals Morris et al [127] offer a more refined framework by establishing five levels of autonomy for AI At the most basic level, AI as a tool involves human oversight, with AI automating routine subtasks AI as a consultant
assumes a substantive but reactive role, engaged only when requested by humans AI as a collaborator enables an
equal partnership between humans and AI, with interactive coordination of goals and tasks AI as an expert takes the
lead in interactions, while humans provide guidance or perform supporting tasks At the highest level, AI as an agent
operates fully autonomously In the context of scientific research, Gao et al

At the highest level, AI as an agent
operates fully autonomously In the context of scientific research, Gao et al [38] introduce three emerging roles of AI
in terms of levels of autonomy, hypothesis creation, experimental planning, reasoning steps, and extent of human-AI
collaboration These are the roles of AI agents as assistants, AI agents as collaborators, and AI agents as scientists From
a mission to enhance productivity and objectivity in scientific studies by circumventing human limitations, Messeri
and Crockett [124] present four AI visions grounded on enhancing human scientists’ capacities along the research
process: oracle, surrogate, quant, and arbiter reflecting stages of research design, data collection, data analysis, and peer
reviewing respectively Driven by the paradigm shift in scientific discovery brought about by LLMs, Zheng et al [228]
propose three levels of LLM autonomy in scientific discovery: tool, analyst, and scientist At the tool level, LLMs
enhance research efficiency through task automation; at the analyst level, they demonstrate significant autonomy in data
modeling and insight generation; at the scientist level, they achieve independent exploration and discovery throughout
key research stages Meanwhile, Zhang et al [218] argue that LLMs introduce a scaling law to scientific discovery and
advance an AGS framework that classifies AI-driven robotic systems into six levels of capability and autonomy, ranging
from no AI involvement to fully autonomous leadership surpassing human scientists This model spans from traditional
methods devoid of AI to the ultimate stage, where artificial superintelligent robots autonomously develop new scientific
paradigms without technological or ethical constraints In view of the increasing autonomy and research participation of LLMs, as well as the urgent need to clarify the
evolving relationship between human researchers and AI in scientific innovation, this study proposes a pyramidal
framework for the roles of LLMs in scientific innovation, as illustrated in Figure 4 and Table 2

scientific competitions The benchmark systematically evaluates eight logical reasoning skills including deductive,
inductive, and causal reasoning, while integrating multimodal elements to test spatial, symbolic, and quantitative

setting and introduces the L3Score metric to assess semantic quality of reasoning outputs GPQA [145] challenges models with 448 graduate-level multiple-choice questions in biology, physics, and chemistry
that demand specialized domain reasoning beyond internet-searchable knowledge Questions are created and validated
by PhD-level experts, targeting complex reasoning about specialized scientific concepts requiring multi-step logical

curated by biology experts The benchmark assesses three key capabilities: expert image understanding, hypothesis
generation, and experiment proposal across diverse microscopy modalities and biological scales CURIE [22] evaluates LLMs’ ability to understand and reason over long-context scientific materials from six diverse
domains including materials science and biodiversity The benchmark comprises ten tasks requiring deep domain
expertise, full paper comprehension, and solution generation in mixed formats including natural language, JSON, and
code SciArena-Eval [227] presents a meta-evaluation benchmark constructed from human preference data to assess model-

The benchmark comprises ten tasks requiring deep domain
expertise, full paper comprehension, and solution generation in mixed formats including natural language, JSON, and
code SciArena-Eval [227] presents a meta-evaluation benchmark constructed from human preference data to assess model-
based evaluators’ alignment with expert judgments on scientific literature tasks The benchmark comprises 2,000
examples across four scientific disciplines, measuring automated evaluation systems’ accuracy in identifying superior
citation-attributed responses compared to human researcher preferences Critical Perspective and Future Dataset Design Taken together, the above reasoning benchmarks delineate a graded
evaluation ladder that spans from elementary multimodal QA to expert-level, long-context scientific problem solving Large-scale resources such as ScienceQA and SPIQA ensure statistical reliability but rely heavily on multiple-choice
formats that cannot expose reasoning chains in depth, while smaller expert suites such as CURIE or GPQA deliver
authentic research difficulty at the cost of coverage and annotation expense Cross–disciplinary sets (e.g., SciEval,
OlympicArena) probe transfer and abstraction, yet inevitably sacrifice domain granularity; conversely, narrowly scoped
collections (e.g., MathVista, MicroVQA) offer fine-grained diagnostics but risk overfitting to siloed skills When
selecting a benchmark, we therefore recommend a three–step fit analysis: scenario alignment—match the cognitive
target (basic comprehension vs graduate reasoning); modality necessity—choose text–only data for pure symbolic
reasoning or multimodal suites for vision–language pipelines; and granularity budget—employ large MCQ sets for
coarse screening, then refine with open-ended expert tasks for error attribution

selecting a benchmark, we therefore recommend a three–step fit analysis: scenario alignment—match the cognitive
target (basic comprehension vs graduate reasoning); modality necessity—choose text–only data for pure symbolic
reasoning or multimodal suites for vision–language pipelines; and granularity budget—employ large MCQ sets for
coarse screening, then refine with open-ended expert tasks for error attribution New benchmarks should integrate
executable outputs (code, equations) alongside natural language to measure verifiable reasoning, embed the full scientific
workflow (hypothesis →experiment →claim) to evaluate process fidelity rather than answer accuracy alone, and adopt
semi-automatic annotation pipelines blended with expert auditing to scale difficulty without prohibitive cost Such
directions will close the current gap between benchmarked capability and real-world scientific practice (2) Scholarly Survey Generation

approaches SciReviewGen [75] formulates literature review generation as a query-focused multi-document summarization task The dataset comprises 10,269 computer science reviews and over 698,000 cited papers, enabling the development and

(1) Scientific Knowledge Reasoning
Scientific innovation largely depends on the ability to synthesize complex information, apply specialized knowledge,
and conduct advanced reasoning across different domains Scientific knowledge reasoning constitutes the cornerstone
of this process [ 22] Compared to knowledge bases, LLMs are considered more suitable for scientific knowledge
reasoning despite their inherent susceptibility to hallucinations [ 172] Based on knowledge types, we categorize
LLM-based scientific knowledge reasoning into explicit knowledge extraction and implicit knowledge reasoning, while
also exploring the explainability of knowledge reasoning [21] Explicit Scientific Knowledge Extraction Scientific literature contains directly visible structured information requiring
systematic extraction This process divides into fine-grained knowledge extraction and key-insights extraction 11

Fine-grained knowledge extraction retrieves specific entities and relationships from scientific text Natural language
processing represents the most extensively explored domain for fine-grained extraction

texts The system leverages transformers like AIONER and LinkBERT to recognize entities and extract relationships This creates a precomputed knowledge graph enabling efficient queries In materials science, Dagdelen et al [23]
implements a generalizable framework using fine-tuned LLMs This approach jointly extracts named entities and
relationships at both sentence and document levels The framework constructs structured knowledge bases from domain
literature using GPT-3 and LLaMA-2 models Key-insights extraction identifies valuable research information within scientific articles This includes research
problems, methods, evaluations, results, limitations, and contributions [ 216,160] Lahav et al [80] focuses specifically
on extracting scientific challenges and research directions Their method uses a PubMedBERT-trained classifier to extract
high-confidence challenges from the CORD-19 dataset Users can retrieve scientific directions through context-based
search inputs Complementing this approach, La Quatra and Cagliero [79] develops THExt, a transformer-based model
generating highlight sentences from academic papers The model employs section-level contextualization to identify key
insights Chao et al [17] proposes SciContriExt, an extractive approach for scientific contributions This model defines
8 contribution types and 15 fine-grained arguments through a keyword-attention fusion mechanism For comprehensive
scientific workflow extraction, Zhang et al [220] construct the MASSW dataset This resource contains over 152,000
structured scientific workflows from 17 prestigious computer science conferences (1969-2024) Using GPT-4, MASSW
systematically organizes five components: Context, Key Idea, Method, Outcome, and Projected Impact This structured
benchmark facilitates efficient navigation of scientific innovation and accelerates methodology replication Song et al

This structured
benchmark facilitates efficient navigation of scientific innovation and accelerates methodology replication Song et al [160] extends these approaches by using multiple fine-tuned open-source LLMs This method automatically extracts
comprehensive key information including aim, motivation, methods, metrics, findings, contributions, limitations, and
future work Implicit Scientific Knowledge Reasoning Unlike explicit knowledge extraction, implicit scientific knowledge
reasoning requires sophisticated multi-hop inference processes that apply domain-specific reasoning principles to derive
unstated conclusions from given information This paradigm demands models to understand intricate scientific concepts,
navigate multi-layered logical dependencies, and generate interpretable explanations while maintaining factual accuracy Current algorithms for implicit scientific knowledge reasoning can be categorized into three fundamental approaches:
Chain-of-Thought reasoning, tool-augmented reasoning, and multimodal knowledge-enhanced reasoning Chain-of-Thought reasoning establishes the foundational paradigm for implicit knowledge reasoning by enhancing
language models’ reasoning capabilities through step-by-step intermediate reasoning generation [ 192] Jin et al [70] introduce explicit thought chain generation through language models that produce lectures and explanations as
intermediate reasoning steps for science question answering Zhang et al [217] advance this paradigm through a
self-reflective instruction annotation framework employing a critic-and-revise mechanism GPT-4 iteratively generates,
analyzes errors, and refines reasoning chains through three sequential stages: initial generation, reflection-based
revision, and answer-hint integration Complex pipelines have also been proposed Zheng et al [229] present a
four-stage LLM4SD pipeline encompassing knowledge synthesis from scientific literature, knowledge inference from
data, interpretable model training, and explanation generation Zhong et al

[229] present a
four-stage LLM4SD pipeline encompassing knowledge synthesis from scientific literature, knowledge inference from
data, interpretable model training, and explanation generation Zhong et al [230] develop a dual-component D5 system
with hypothesis proposer utilizing goal-conditioned prompting and hypothesis validator employing automated validity
assessment Furthermore, based on curated reasoning samples for training reasoning models, Prabhakar et al [137]
implement a three-step algorithmic pipeline comprising Domain Adaptive Pretraining on curated scientific corpora,
Supervised Fine-Tuning with instruction alignment, and reasoning-based knowledge distillation to enhance logical
synthesis capabilities Tool-augmented reasoning creates modular frameworks for implicit scientific knowledge reasoning, positioning LLMs
as proficient tool-users capable of extending domain applicability rather than omniscient problem solvers Wang
et al [177] introduce the LCE (Language, Code, Execution) framework that seamlessly interleaves natural language
reasoning with code generation and real-time execution feedback through special token demarcation Ma et al [121]
propose a four-module algorithmic architecture comprising Planning, Retrieval, Action, and Execution components,
where domain-specific toolsets are dynamically retrieved and executed based on problem requirements Skarlinski et al 12

[157] develop an agentic Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) algorithm that decomposes retrieval and response
generation into specialized tools including Paper Search, Gather Evidence, and Generate Answer, enabling iterative
search refinement through citation graph traversal and contextual summarization Multimodal knowledge-enhanced reasoning integrates knowledge from diverse modalities including text, images,
and structured knowledge networks to provide rich contextual background and verifiable traceability for implicit
knowledge reasoning Scientific papers extensively utilize tables and figures to communicate complex information [ 57]

Multimodal knowledge-enhanced reasoning integrates knowledge from diverse modalities including text, images,
and structured knowledge networks to provide rich contextual background and verifiable traceability for implicit
knowledge reasoning Scientific papers extensively utilize tables and figures to communicate complex information [ 57] These elements contain implicit knowledge requiring multimodal fusion for effective reasoning Zhang et al [224]
propose a two-stage Multimodal-CoT framework separating rationale generation from answer inference to effectively
leverage multimodal information Wang et al [178] develop T-SciQ with dual teaching signal generation algorithms
combining QA-CoT for simple problems and QA-PCoT for complex multi-step reasoning through strategic data mixing
optimization Jin et al [70] introduce HeGTa, employing Heterogeneous Graph Neural Networks to model complex
table relationships through four node types and heuristic edge creation rules, integrated with LLMs via soft prompt
injection for few-shot complex table understanding Mondal et al [126] propose KAM-CoT that decomposes complex
problems into multiple intermediate steps through Chain-of-Thought reasoning, separately encodes text, images, and
Knowledge Graphs and fuses them into unified feature sets for comprehensive task understanding, finally providing
accurate and reasonable answers through a two-stage approach of rationale generation and answer inference Critical Perspective and Future Algorithm Design Present methods form a complementary spectrum Explicit
extraction pipelines (e.g., PubTator 3.0, MASSW) deliver high-precision, auditable triples and are easily aggregated
into knowledge graphs, yet they depend on costly annotation, propagate NER/RE errors, and cannot surface latent
mechanisms Chain-of-Thought reasoning brings interpretability, but is brittle: Erroneous early steps snowball, and
self-critique is still heuristic

Explicit
extraction pipelines (e.g., PubTator 3.0, MASSW) deliver high-precision, auditable triples and are easily aggregated
into knowledge graphs, yet they depend on costly annotation, propagate NER/RE errors, and cannot surface latent
mechanisms Chain-of-Thought reasoning brings interpretability, but is brittle: Erroneous early steps snowball, and
self-critique is still heuristic Tool-augmented frameworks (LCE, SciAgent) tame hallucination by delegating calculus,
retrieval, or code execution to external tools, but orchestration logic is cumbersome and failure modes multiply with tool
count Multimodal reasoning (Multimodal-CoT, KAM-CoT) uniquely captures figure- and table-bound insights, yet
training costs and modality alignment remain prohibitive Algorithm selection should align with task demands: explicit
extraction best suits verifiable database construction; Chain-of-Thought methods are preferable for fast, explanatory
problem solving; tool-augmented agents fit numerically intensive or data-hungry settings; and multimodal hybrids are
recommended for vision-rich corpora Future work should fuse extraction and reasoning through retrieval-augmented
Chain-of-Thought coupled with automatic verifiers, embed confidence calibration and contradiction checks to halt error
propagation, develop plug-and-play tool registries with self-discovery and fallback logic, and design unified scientific
embeddings that treat equations, spectra, and graphics as first-class citizens, enabling truly modality-agnostic reasoning (2) Scholarly Survey Generation
Literature reviews represent structured approaches to scientific knowledge synthesis They consolidate and analyze
existing research across various domains These reviews divide into three categories based on purpose, research
questions, search strategy, analysis methods, and contributions [ 158] Systematic literature reviews apply explicit
methodical approaches to examine evidence addressing specific research questions

These reviews divide into three categories based on purpose, research
questions, search strategy, analysis methods, and contributions [ 158] Systematic literature reviews apply explicit
methodical approaches to examine evidence addressing specific research questions Semi-systematic reviews provide
topic overviews and track historical development of diversely conceptualized subjects Integrative literature reviews
involve creative, interpretative analysis [ 129] For mature topics, integrative reviews summarize knowledge bases,
critically evaluate findings, and expand theoretical foundations For emerging topics, they develop preliminary
conceptualizations and theoretical models Current LLM-supported survey generation primarily focuses on systematic
or semi-systematic reviews The development of integrative literature reviews based on qualitative analysis remains
underdeveloped LLM-supported literature review automation employs two distinct methodological approaches The
first approach organizes literature into structured formats such as hierarchical structures or layered classifications This
organization facilitates effective review generation The second approach builds end-to-end systems with modules that
simulate human review-writing processes These processes include literature retrieval, screening, classification, drafting,
integration, and evaluation Structured Literature Organization Approach Kang and Xiong [73] categorize the use of LLMs in academic litera-
ture reviews into three steps: information discovery, information selection, and information organization Structuring
knowledge into hierarchical mind maps highlights key insights and relationships in research topics while improving
linguistic coherence Hu et al [56] propose HiGTL, a framework integrating Graph Neural Networks and LLMs It gen-
erates hierarchical taxonomies from citation graphs by clustering papers based on structural and semantic relationships Using pre-trained LLMs, it provides natural language representations of classification nodes, offering a clear overview
of research trends Hsu et al

Using pre-trained LLMs, it provides natural language representations of classification nodes, offering a clear overview
of research trends Hsu et al [53] introduce CHIME, which employs LLMs to organize biomedical research into
hierarchical category trees This system extracts concise claims and frequent entities from abstracts and uses Claude-2
to create topic-specific hierarchies, presenting categories as nodes and studies as leaves, thus enhancing researchers’
ability to navigate and synthesize literature Newman et al [131] employs LLMs to create literature review tables These
tables synthesize multiple input papers into a structure with patterns (columns) and values Researchers can effectively
13

compare papers across consistent dimensions They decompose this complex task into two key components First,
structure generation identifies relevant shared aspects (columns) from input papers Second, value generation extracts
appropriate values for each paper-aspect combination Furthermore, Wang et al [184] address real-world literature
review scenarios that contain noisy, irrelevant papers and under-specified user demands They develop an iterative
batch-based table generation method This approach specifically includes using LLMs to extract key information from
full-text content, processing papers in batches through random partitioning, and iterative paper selection and schema
refinement Beyond hierarchical approaches, Nishimura et al [132] develop STRoGeNS, a method for generating multi-paragraph,
structured related work sections with citations and novelty statements It groups literature by research topics and
emphasizes the target paper’s novelty, ensuring coherence and informativeness Li et al [90] argue that simple chain-
of-thought methods and model limitations cause LLM-generated summaries to lack comparative analysis, structure,
and key elements To address this, they introduce ChatCite, which mimics human literature comparison workflows

[90] argue that simple chain-
of-thought methods and model limitations cause LLM-generated summaries to lack comparative analysis, structure,
and key elements To address this, they introduce ChatCite, which mimics human literature comparison workflows It
features a key element extractor using seven guiding questions to identify critical details and a reflective incremental
generator with two components: a comparative summarizer for iterative summary generation via comparative analysis,
and a reflective evaluator that uses LLMs to vote, screen, and rank candidate papers Zhang et al [223] propose
Collaborative Knowledge Minigraph Agents (CKMAs) to automate scholarly literature reviews through graph-based
approach This framework employs a Knowledge Minigraph Construction Agent (KMCA) that uses prompt-based
algorithms to identify relations between scientific concepts and automatically construct small-scale knowledge graphs
specific to the referenced papers Combined with a Multiple Path Summarization Agent (MPSA) that organizes concepts
from different viewpoints using a mixture of experts approach, the system efficiently generates comprehensive literature
reviews End-to-End Survey Generation Systems Recent research focuses on automating traditional manual review processes
while addressing challenges of hallucination, knowledge evolution, and domain-specific comprehension Integrating
RAG, Shi et al [154] introduces UR3WG, a unified framework for reference retrieval and related work generation This
model employs query expansion with LLMs to capture implicit context and specialized terminology The framework’s
Lexicon-Enhanced Retrieval combines semantic similarity with lexical-level matching, utilizing multi-granularity
contrastive learning to enhance retrieval accuracy Similarly, Agarwal et al [1]develops LitLLM, an open-source
toolkit for automatic literature review generation using RAG and LLMs

Similarly, Agarwal et al [1]develops LitLLM, an open-source
toolkit for automatic literature review generation using RAG and LLMs LitLLM’s modular pipeline includes retrieval,
re-ranking, and generation phases, focusing on mitigating hallucinations by grounding the process in retrieved academic
papers The toolkit offers zero-shot and plan-based generation options, enabling customized outputs based on user
requirements Further, Susnjak et al [166] automates the process through domain-specific fine-tuning of LLMs Their
approach encompasses automatic data extraction at multiple levels and introduces unique tokens for tracking source
document responses Their fine-tuned Mistral-7B models, particularly those utilizing NEFTune and LoRA techniques,
demonstrate superior performance in factual verification compared to pure RAG approaches End-to-end literature review generation systems continue to emerge Wang et al [186] creates AutoSurvey, address-
ing challenges of extensive research volumes and rapid publication rates To overcome context window limitations,
AutoSurvey employs a four-stage pipeline: initial retrieval and outline generation, parallel subsection drafting, integra-
tion, and multi-model evaluation The system generates high-quality surveys 1000 times faster than human authors
while maintaining comparable content quality Liang et al [91] introduces SurveyX with a two-phase pipeline The
preparation stage utilizes keyword expansion algorithms for reference retrieval and structures citation information
into attribute trees The generation phase executes outline generation, main body generation, and post refinement
(RAG-based Rewriting Module and Figure/Table Generation Module) Compared to AutoSurvey, SurveyX achieves
measurable improvements in content quality and citation quality Given that LLM-generated outlines lack logical flow
and structural depth, and citations are inaccurate due to hallucinations, Yan et al [202] propose frameworks named
SurveyForge This framework combines heuristic outline generation with memory-driven content generation

[202] propose frameworks named
SurveyForge This framework combines heuristic outline generation with memory-driven content generation By
analyzing human-written survey structures and integrating domain-specific articles to create balanced, hierarchical
outlines, it then employs a scholar navigation agent that decomposes complex queries into sub-queries using domain
literature This agent prioritizes influential papers using citation counts and recency, ensuring cited literature is both
relevant and impactful, outperforming AutoSurvey in reference coverage, outline quality, and average content quality Critical Perspective and Future Algorithm Design Two design philosophies dominate Structured-organization
approaches (HiGTL, CHIME, arXivDIGESTables) excel at taxonomy clarity and cross-paper comparability, but often
omit nuanced critique, require upstream extraction accuracy, and struggle with topics lacking clear hierarchies In
contrast, end-to-end systems (AutoSurvey, SurveyX, SurveyForge) offer hour-scale draft generation and flexible
coverage, yet still hallucinate citations, drift logically across sections, and underperform on deep synthesis or critical
appraisal Choice hinges on purpose: structured pipelines are ideal for pedagogical maps or decision trees; end-to-end
retrieval-augmented systems suffice for rapid domain scans or first-pass reviews; a hybrid that layers structured outlining
atop iterative, retrieval-grounded drafting is necessary when both breadth and depth are required Next-generation survey
14

engines should pair citation-aware planners with real-time fact-checkers to reduce hallucinations, track concept evolution
so that reviews remain current as literature grows, introduce multi-agent critique loops that combine summarization
with adversarial questioning to deepen analysis, and learn quality-weighted reward functions—such as the SAM-R/O/C
suite—to guide models toward authoritative, well-structured, and insightful surveys
