In mathematics, evaluations showcase the potential of LLMs to advance fundamental research. FunSearch achieved a
landmark breakthrough by discovering the largest known cap set in 8 dimensions (512 vectors). This represents the first
improvement in this dimension and a 20-year advancement in asymptotic lower bounds for cap set capacity [ 147]. In
equation discovery, LLM4ED demonstrated remarkable accuracy with coefficient errors below 1.5% for most partial
differential equation systems. It achieved over 90% R2scores on both training and test sets for ordinary differential
equations [ 29]. The LLM-SR framework significantly outperformed traditional symbolic regression baselines. It
particularly excelled in out-of-domain generalization scenarios, maintaining superior performance even under noisy
conditions [156].
In more comprehensive cross-disciplinary evaluations, current LLM-based autonomous scientific discovery systems
reveal significant limitations despite their potential. DiscoveryBench, which covers six diverse domains, found that even
the best performing system achieved only a 25% Hypothesis Matching Score. Performance was strongly correlated with
workflow complexity and domain-specific expertise requirements [ 122]. The evaluation of ScienceAgentBench across
four scientific disciplines showed that the highest performing agent could solve only 32.4% of the tasks independently.
It reached 42.2% with OpenAI o1-preview but at ten times the computational cost [ 20]. DiscoveryWorld’s virtual
environment for complete scientific discovery cycles found that strong baseline agents struggled on most tasks. This
suggests fundamental gaps in end-to-end scientific reasoning capabilities [ 67]. In particular, even in neuroscience
prediction tasks where LLM achieved 81.4% accuracy compared to 63.4% of human experts, the evaluation focused on
pattern recognition rather than genuine hypothesis generation [112].
5.4 Observations
LLMs are increasingly formalized as scientists with two concentric mandates. Autonomous Scientific Research seeks
to optimize established procedures, including literature review, experiment planning, execution, and reporting, while
Autonomous Scientific Discovery pursues genuinely novel findings that extend the frontier of human knowledge. Despite
sharing many algorithmic primitives, such as multi-agent orchestration, tool integration, and closed-loop verification,
the two modes diverge in objectives, risk profiles, and evidentiary standards. This reveals both complementary strengths
and common methodological gaps.
Autonomous Scientific Research:
Capabilities
•End-to-end automation markedly reduces turnaround time and cost for routine analytical workflows, from data
ingestion to manuscript drafting.
•Iterative, feedback-driven loops allow agents to refine code and experimental parameters without continuous
human intervention.
•Retrieval-augmented reasoning enables more comprehensive literature coverage and context-aware decision-
making.
Limitations
•Deep domain reasoning—particularly equation verification, protocol nuance, and multimodal interpreta-
tion—remains brittle, limiting trust in unaudited outputs.
•Errors introduced early in monolithic pipelines can propagate unchecked; embedded, independent verification
layers are still nascent.
•Coordination overhead in multi-agent settings inflates computational cost and complicates provenance tracking,
especially in safety-critical domains.
Autonomous Scientific Discovery:
Capabilities
•Generative search over hypothesis space, coupled with programmatic verifiers or simulators, has yielded
demonstrable advances in mathematics, materials science, and chemistry.
•Role-specialized LLM laboratories (planner, critic, coder, experimenter) foster internal peer review and
diversify exploratory trajectories.
•Evolutionary and symbolic-regression pipelines enforce falsifiability by separating generation from external
evaluation.
46

Limitations
•Scalable validating large volumes of candidate hypotheses remains costly; partial checks risk false-positive
discoveries.
•Search procedures can converge prematurely on local optima, necessitating explicit diversity preservation and
adaptive exploration strategies.
•Cross-domain generalization is limited: systems proficient in, say, algebraic conjecture often stumble in
biological inference, underscoring the need for transferable reasoning scaffolds.
ASR systems already deliver practical efficiency gains for well-defined tasks, while ASD frameworks exhibit isolated
but compelling breakthroughs. Both strands, however, confront fundamental issues of robust reasoning, verification
rigor, and accountable deployment. Future research should priorities modular architectures that decouple ideation,
execution, and validation; incorporate uncertainty quantification; and embed cryptographically secure provenance to
enable reproducible, trustworthy autonomous science.
6 Discussion
6.1 Ethical Considerations and Safety
Ethics. The integration of LLMs into scientific innovation introduces significant ethical challenges. LLM-driven
advances may cause researchers to overestimate their true understanding of scientific phenomena, as AI-generated
explanations often appear highly persuasive. Reliance on LLMs can also foster scientific monocultures, narrowing
methodological diversity and limiting the breadth of exploratory inquiry. Furthermore, the intrinsic biases present
in LLMs risk perpetuating societal prejudices and algorithmic unfairness, which may intensify existing inequalities
[124,19,228]. As LLMs increasingly assume autonomous roles in scientific innovation, additional ethical risks emerge,
including threats to data privacy, potential content fabrication, increased risk of plagiarism, and a reduction in critical
human oversight. Collectively, these issues pose a substantial threat to scientific integrity, create opportunities for novel
forms of misuse, and complicate accountability and responsibility within the innovation process [34, 146].
Addressing these challenges requires establishing inclusive and adaptive governance frameworks that embed trans-
parency, accountability, and continuous ethical reflection into the design and deployment of LLM-driven scientific
innovations [ 82,218]. Ensuring scholarly integrity demands that researchers retain sufficient oversight and account-
ability over innovations facilitated by LLMs, thus safeguarding the reliability and validity of scientific outcomes.
Additionally, scientific innovations driven by LLMs should be guided explicitly toward benefiting the common good.
Adopting this broader sociotechnical perspective involves active public deliberation, recognition and integration of
diverse values, and continuous alignment with established ethical principles and international standards.
Safety. In addition to ethical concerns, significant safety risks arise from the growing autonomy and capabilities
of AI scientist systems. As LLMs increasingly undertake critical tasks such as hypothesis generation, experimental
design, and manuscript preparation, new risks emerge, including insufficient human oversight, potential misdirection of
scientific efforts, and the inadvertent automation of flawed research protocols [ 201,19]. Without adequate oversight,
errors or biased results produced by LLMs could remain unnoticed, emphasizing the necessity of robust governance
frameworks, transparent documentation processes, and clear attribution mechanisms throughout the scientific innovation
lifecycle.
Further, as LLM-driven innovation approaches higher levels of sophisticated agentic behaviors, potential safety threats
such as misaligned objectives, self-preservation tendencies, and deceptive actions become increasingly prominent [ 7].
These threats necessitate careful design principles that emphasize interpretability, uncertainty modeling, and explicit
constraints on autonomous decision-making. Collaborative frameworks emphasizing consistent human oversight will
be crucial to ensuring safe, responsible, and effective scientific innovation.
6.2 Challenges and Future Directions
6.2.1 Core Challenges
Model Capability and Reliability Limitations. LLMs face three tightly coupled obstacles: hallucination and factual
accuracy, domain-specific comprehension, and out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization, which together constitute the
most fundamental barrier to AI-enabled scientific innovation. First, the autoregressive training paradigm makes LLMs
prone to producing outputs that sound plausible yet are objectively false, such as citing irrelevant or nonexistent papers
during literature surveys [ 222,221]. These false results are especially dangerous in high-risk laboratory settings, where
47

they can lead to erroneous protocols and uncontrolled experimental execution [ 221]. Second, current models often fail
to grasp specialized terminology and complex concepts, for example, by misjudging critical protein-protein interactions
in biochemistry or overlooking subtle mathematical assumptions in theoretical physics [ 116]. Moreover, most scientific
LLMs are trained at a coarse field level (e.g. “chemistry”), leaving long-tailed, fine-grained topics insufficiently covered
[222]. Third, scientific test distributions routinely diverge from training data; newly coined concepts, unseen molecular
scaffolds, or proteins with novel chain counts emerge continuously, and current pretrained LLMs still struggle to handle
such shifts [222].
Lack of Transparency and Explainability. The black-box nature of current LLMs undermines scientific validation,
trust, and assimilation of AI-driven insights [ 228]. Overcoming this opacity requires a paradigm shift toward architec-
tures designed for verifiable reasoning and provable conclusions rather than superficial post hoc explanations [ 228]. In
addition, even with enlarged context windows, models often lose coherence when analyzing lengthy manuscripts, often
missing cross-sectional logical dependencies [116].
Multimodal and Multilingual Integration Difficulties. Scientific corpora span manuscripts, high-resolution images,
time series signals, code, and structured tables; each modality requires bespoke preprocessing, yet high-quality cross-
modal alignments are extremely scarce, particularly in expert-intensive domains, generating training and evaluation
costs [ 57,19]. Moreover, the English-centric bias of existing LLMs risks overlooking low-resource research areas and
hampers the integration of global data and expertise needed to tackle worldwide challenges such as COVID-19 [19].
Benchmark and Evaluation Bottlenecks. Most publicly available suites remain static, allowing models to overfit
through exposure in pre-training corpora and leaderboard gaming [ 165]. Even the newest collections seldom mirror the
full closed loop of scientific practice, from hypothesis generation to experimental verification, so systems that excel at
multiple choice or code writing subtasks routinely fail when asked to design, execute and interpret real experiments
[72]. Leakage further undermines credibility: many test questions are paraphrases of highly cited papers, making it
difficult to disentangle genuine reasoning from memorization [ 107]. Disciplinary coverage is also skewed; biology,
chemistry, and computer science dominate, whereas low-resource fields such as ecology or the social sciences receive
minimal representation, producing inflated aggregate scores that mask domain-specific weaknesses [ 122]. Multimodality
compounds the problem: vision–language tasks rarely include raw spectra, micrographs, or CAD files, so cross-modal
reasoning remains largely untested [ 81]. Finally, current leaderboards overwhelmingly reward answer accuracy,
neglecting critical dimensions such as novelty, energy cost, carbon footprint, and reproducibility, thereby encouraging
incremental gains rather than scientifically meaningful progress [ 20]. Addressing these shortcomings will require
continually refreshed, leak-resistant benchmarks that grade entire research pipelines, incorporate under-represented
modalities and disciplines, and report multi-objective metrics aligned with real scientific value.
6.2.2 Future Directions
Domain-Specific Knowledgeable Models. Future language-model development is expected to shift from broad,
“one-size-fits-all” systems toward deeply specialized models whose tokenisation schemes, pre-training corpora and
reasoning mechanisms are explicitly aligned with the primitives, ontologies and evaluation protocols of a single scientific
discipline, because empirical evidence already shows that using function-infused molecular building blocks rather than
atom-level tokens improves chemical reasoning and synthesizability [ 33], and a cross-field meta-analysis of more than
260 scientific LLMs demonstrates that performance gains are consistently largest when models are pre-trained and
benchmarked on field-specific data and tasks [222].
Integration with the Physical World. Forthcoming LLMs are expected to evolve into autonomous research
agents that couple high-level reasoning with direct laboratory control, thereby establishing a closed hypothe-
sis–experiment–data–hypothesis loop without human intervention [ 228]. Embedding planning modules in robotic
platforms gives rise to “robot scientists” capable of generating, executing, and continually refining chemical syntheses
or materials-characterization protocols [ 228]. When equipped with real-time sensing and online reinforcement learning,
such systems constitute self-driving laboratories that perform millisecond-scale feedback optimization, dramatically
reducing the search space for novel compounds and process parameters [ 19]. Moreover, embodied hybrid LLM-robot
can conduct in situ experimentation in extreme environments, deep oceans, high-radiation zones, or extraterrestrial ter-
rains, beyond the limits of human physiology [ 218]. A dual-domain workflow that screens hypotheses via high-fidelity
simulation before robotic validation further decreases experimental cost while increasing success rates [228].
Cross-Disciplinary Agent Networks. Complex scientific challenges increasingly demand knowledge that spans
multiple fields, motivating the development of multi-agent LLM networks in which domain-specialized agents cooperate
through structured message passing to execute elaborate research workflows [ 19]. Graph-based knowledge routing
enables hypotheses, variables, and results to traverse disciplinary boundaries, mitigating information silos and deepening
causal inference [ 233]. Privacy-preserving federated learning allows geographically distributed institutions to co-train
foundation models while retaining local data sovereignty, thus expanding cross-domain sample diversity without
48

compromising compliance [ 19]. Within these networks, agents dynamically assume roles in hypothesis generation,
protocol design, and data interpretation, which optimizes resource allocation and accelerates iterative discovery cycles
[228].
Human–AI Collaborative Scholarly Ecosystems. LLM agents will also reshape the social infrastructure of science
by fostering AI-native publication and review platforms. Pre-print servers such as the proposed AgentRxiv would
institute tiered review pipelines tailored to outputs generated autonomously by AI or robot scientists, guaranteeing
transparency, traceability, and ethical oversight [ 31,218]. Concurrently, intelligent peer-review assistants can flag
methodological flaws, verify citations, and deliver structured critiques, thereby decreasing reviewer workload while
maintaining scholarly rigor [ 116]. End-to-end dashboards that expose an LLM’s reasoning chain and confidence
estimates promote interoperability and enable real-time auditing of AI-derived insights [ 228]. Finally, integrating
high-quality multilingual translation and terminology alignment modules ensures equitable visibility for research in
low-resource languages, narrowing the global knowledge divide and enriching the collective scientific corpus [19].
7 Conclusion
This paper delivers a comprehensive and unified survey of the ways in which LLMs are reshaping scientific innovation.
Guided by three criteria, autonomy, task complexity, and human-AI collaboration, we position LLM capabilities within
a three-level pyramid comprising the roles of Evaluator, Collaborator, and Scientist. At the dimensions of benchmarks,
algorithms, and evaluation and results, we detail the capabilities and limitations of Evaluators in scientific knowledge
synthesis and literature quality assessment, Collaborators in hypothesis generation and experimental assistance, and
Scientists in autonomous research and discovery. The review also examines ethical considerations, identifies potential
safety risks, and outlines productive avenues for future work. We hope that this survey will serve as a practical reference
for researchers seeking to understand and responsibly advance LLM-driven scientific innovation.
